title: Sealed Types, Value Classes, Inheritance, Visibility & Init Order
scopeHtml: Scope: sealed classes and interfaces vs enums, exhaustive when and sealed-hierarchy rules, value classes (boxing, mangling, Java interop), final-by-default and open/abstract, interfaces and JVM default methods, visibility modifiers, nested vs inner classes, anonymous objects, and constructor/initialization order. Data classes, enums in depth, objects and companions belong to K2a. Variance of Result<out T> belongs to K5, and SAM conversions belong to K3b.

notes.title: Enum versus sealed class versus sealed interface
notes.html:
The idea. All three describe "a closed list of possibilities", but at different levels.

  • Enum: a fixed list of instances, all with the same shape. (Monday, Tuesday...)
  • Sealed class: a fixed list of subtypes, each of which can carry different data.
  • Sealed interface: the same, but subtypes are free to extend another class too.
enum sealed class sealed interface
Cases are singleton instances subclasses (objects or classes with fields) implementations (objects or classes)
Data per case same fields for all different per subclass different per implementation
Instances per case exactly one many (for class), one (for object) many or one
Shared state in the parent no yes (constructor, fields) no (only properties as abstract/with getters)
A case can extend another class no no (single parent already used) yes
Compiler knows full list for when yes yes yes
Built-ins values/entries, valueOf, EnumMap none none

Concrete examples.

enum class Plan { FREE, PRO, ENTERPRISE }                          // same shape, a label

sealed class PaymentResult {                                        // different data per case
    data class Success(val receiptId: String) : PaymentResult()
    data class Declined(val reason: String, val retryable: Boolean) : PaymentResult()
    data object Cancelled : PaymentResult()
}

sealed interface FeedItem { val id: Long }                         // cases may have other parents
data class Post(override val id: Long, val text: String) : FeedItem, Serializable
data class Ad(override val id: Long, val sponsor: String) : FeedItem, Parcelable

How to choose. Same shape and a persistent/serialised value: enum (plus a stable code). Different payload per case (UI state, network result, navigation event, MVI intent): sealed. Need a case to also be Parcelable, Serializable, or extend a Message base: sealed interface. A sealed class adds a shared constructor/field you want in every case (e.g. sealed class Event(val timestamp: Long)).

Bytecode. A sealed class is abstract with a private/protected constructor (so Java and other modules cannot extend it); on JVM target 17 and above the compiler also writes a PermittedSubclasses attribute so Java 17 recognises it as sealed. A sealed interface is an interface plus the same attribute.

Industry usage. Google's Now in Android and countless MVVM apps model UiState as sealed interface { Loading; Success; Error }; Retrofit-style wrappers (ApiResult), Kotlin's own Result-like types, Navigation 2.8 type-safe routes, kotlinx.coroutines ChannelResult.

Real-life picture. A restaurant: the enum is the set of table numbers (all tables look alike, one name each). A sealed class is the kinds of customer order (dine-in with a table, takeaway with a pickup time, delivery with an address): each needs different information.

Common interview traps.

  • Using an enum when cases need different fields (leading to nullable fields everywhere).
  • Using a sealed class when a case must also extend another class (use sealed interface).
  • Saying sealed classes are "enums with data": sealed classes can have many instances per case.

notes.title: Exhaustive when and adding a subclass
notes.html:
The idea. Because the compiler knows the full list of sealed subtypes, a when that handles all of them needs no else. When someone adds a subtype, every non-updated when stops compiling, which tells you where to work.

fun message(r: PaymentResult): String = when (r) {
    is PaymentResult.Success   -> "Paid: ${r.receiptId}"      // smart cast to Success
    is PaymentResult.Declined  -> "Declined: ${r.reason}"
    PaymentResult.Cancelled    -> "Cancelled"                  // data object: equality, no 'is'
}

Rules.

  • Exhaustiveness is required when when is used as an expression, and (since Kotlin 1.7) also for when statements over sealed, enum and Boolean subjects.
  • is is needed for classes; objects can be matched by ==/name. Nested sealed hierarchies must be exhaustively covered at every level (the compiler checks the whole tree, so a sealed subclass's own children are included).
  • Adding else removes the compiler help: a new subtype silently goes to else. Prefer explicit branches on sealed types.

What the bytecode does. A chain of instanceof checks (or equality for objects). For an exhaustive expression without else, the compiler appends a final branch that throws kotlin.NoWhenBranchMatchedException. Normally unreachable, it is reachable when the class hierarchy at runtime differs from the one at compile time (separate compilation, see the cross-module section).

Practical consequence when you add a subclass. In the same module: build fails at each when expression. Tests catch missing mapping. In a multi-module app, other modules depending on yours fail on their next compile. Binary-only consumers fail at runtime.

Real-life picture. A dispatch board listing every kind of ambulance call. When a new kind ("flood rescue") is added, the board flags every dispatcher script that has no instruction for it, instead of letting it fall into "other".

Common interview traps.

  • Believing exhaustiveness also protects code that was compiled against the old hierarchy.
  • Adding else -> Unit "to silence the error".
  • Using when on a val property from another module (smart cast impossible) and getting confused about is.

notes.title: Where sealed subclasses may live
notes.html:
The rules.

  1. Direct subclasses of a sealed class or sealed interface must be declared in the same package and the same module (compiled together) as the sealed type. Since Kotlin 1.5 they may be in different files (before that, the same file only).
  2. Subclasses need not be nested inside the parent: top-level declarations in the package are fine.
  3. Indirect subclasses (a subclass of a non-sealed direct subclass, or an open direct subclass) may be declared anywhere that can see it, in any package or module. The compiler treats the direct subclass as the leaf of the closed list. A direct subclass declared sealed closes its own sub-list.
  4. Constructors of a sealed class are protected by default (never public); sealed classes are implicitly abstract; a sealed class itself cannot be instantiated.
  5. Java cannot extend a Kotlin sealed type (the constructor is inaccessible and the class is marked sealed in bytecode for JVM 17 and above).
  6. Kotlin Multiplatform: a sealed hierarchy must still satisfy the "same module" rule; subclasses may not be spread across arbitrary source sets or modules (confirm the exact source-set rule in the current KMP docs). Local classes and anonymous objects cannot be direct subclasses.
  7. Different from an enum: you cannot add cases from a dependent module. If you need an open-ended list, use an interface (not sealed) or a registry.

Practical modelling tip. To let plugin modules add cases, keep the sealed core small and add an Extension(val payload: Any) or Unknown case; or use an ordinary interface with a Handler registry. Navigation graphs in large apps (Airbnb, Uber style) often use per-feature sealed hierarchies that are combined by an interface Destination.

Industry usage. sealed interface Intent per feature module in MVI; kotlinx.serialization's SerializersModule for open polymorphism when sealed does not fit.

Real-life picture. A family tree for a company's founders, written down once: only people recorded when the tree was drawn are "direct children". Grandchildren can be added anywhere later, but nobody new can be added as a direct child afterwards.

Common interview traps.

  • "Sealed subclasses must be nested in the parent" (old rule, pre-1.5 file rule).
  • Thinking a subclass in another module of the same app is allowed.
  • Forgetting that indirect descendants can be anywhere and are not tracked by when.

notes.title: Sealed hierarchies across modules
notes.html:
The design question. In a multi-module app, a core module defines sealed interface Destination, and feature modules want to add their own screens. The sealed rule forbids that. Options and trade-offs:

Approach Pros Cons
One sealed hierarchy in a shared navigation-api module listing all screens exhaustive when, compile-time safety every feature depends on the shared module; adding a screen touches shared code and triggers rebuilds of all dependents
Per-feature sealed hierarchies + a small open interface at the top features independent, each feature exhaustive internally the top level is not exhaustive
Open interface + Map<KClass, Handler> registry (via Hilt multibindings) extensible, plugin style no compile-time exhaustiveness, missing handler found at runtime

Binary compatibility risk. If a library module publishes a sealed type and an app module whens over it, a library update that adds a subclass breaks callers at runtime if the app is not recompiled (precompiled SDK jar, dynamic feature module, an AAR updated alone): the old when reaches its synthetic else and throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException. Public SDKs (Google Play Billing, Firebase) often avoid sealed in public API or document "this may gain new subtypes: always handle else/Unknown".

Practical rules for libraries.

  • Public sealed hierarchies are part of your API contract; adding a subtype is a source- and binary-breaking change for exhaustive callers.
  • Use @NonExhaustive-style documentation or an Unknown case, or expose an enum-like with UNKNOWN.
  • Add a binary-compatibility validator (kotlinx.binary-compatibility-validator) to CI, and run API-diff in code review.

Real-life picture. A restaurant chain printing menus: if every branch must follow the head office's menu list exactly, a new dish at head office requires reprinting all branch menus; if branches are allowed a "chef's special" line, they cope without a reprint.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting a feature-specific case in a shared sealed hierarchy and creating a god module.
  • Assuming a compile pass means runtime safety when modules ship independently (dynamic features).
  • Using sealed in a public SDK without an Unknown escape hatch.

notes.title: Evolving sealed types with server data
notes.html:
The problem. A backend returns {"type": "carousel", ...}; your sealed hierarchy FeedItem has Banner, Post, Ad. The server team adds "type": "poll" before the new app is rolled out. Old app versions receive a type they do not know.

What breaks, by library.

  • Moshi PolymorphicJsonAdapterFactory.of(FeedItem::class.java, "type") throws JsonDataException: Expected one of [banner, post, ad] for key 'type' but found 'poll' unless you set withDefaultValue(Unknown).
  • kotlinx.serialization throws SerializationException: Class discriminator 'poll' is not registered for polymorphic serialization unless you register polymorphicDefaultDeserializer(FeedItem::class) { UnknownItem.serializer() }.
  • Gson with a custom adapter often returns null, which later crashes a non-null list.

The result is a whole-feed parse failure: one unknown item kills the screen for everyone on old versions (Instagram-style feeds, Spotify home shelves, Swiggy/Zomato home sections all hit this class of problem).

The production pattern.

  1. Add data class Unknown(val type: String) : FeedItem (or data object) to the sealed hierarchy.
  2. Configure the deserializer to fall back to it for unknown tags.
  3. In the UI mapper, drop or hide Unknown (do not render a blank card), but log it (a counter in analytics, not a crash).
  4. Make the parsing per-item tolerant: a bad item becomes Unknown, not a failed list.
  5. Server contract: only add new types behind an app-version/feature flag and keep old clients' payloads valid; use minAppVersion fields.
  6. Test with a recorded payload that contains an unknown type (contract test).

Related enum case. The same applies to enums: UNKNOWN fallback plus coerceInputValues.

Real-life picture. A mail sorter trained on letters and parcels. A new kind of item arrives ("drone box"). Without a "send to supervisor" bin, the sorting line jams; with it, the box is set aside and the line keeps moving.

Common interview traps.

  • Using sealed hierarchy plus strict decoding with no default.
  • Rendering Unknown as an empty card with padding (looks like a bug).
  • Handling Unknown in the parser but still using else in the UI when: handle it explicitly.

notes.title: Final by default: open, abstract and override
notes.html:
The idea. In Kotlin every class and member is final unless you write open. Letting anyone subclass a class means they can break its assumptions; each open member is a promise you keep forever. This follows Effective Java's advice: "design and document for inheritance or else prohibit it".

open class Animal {                // can be extended
    open fun sound() = "..."       // can be overridden
    fun breathe() = "in/out"       // final
}
class Dog : Animal() {
    override fun sound() = "Woof"  // 'override' is itself open
}
class Puppy : Animal() {
    final override fun sound() = "Yip"    // stops further overriding
}

Rules.

  • open on a class enables extension; open on a member enables overriding; both are needed.
  • abstract classes cannot be instantiated and may declare members without bodies; abstract members are implicitly open.
  • override is mandatory (no silent override like Java's @Override optional annotation); an override member is open unless final.
  • Calling the parent: super.sound(); with multiple interface defaults: super<A>.foo().
  • Smart casts depend on this: a property can be smart-cast only if it is final (not open) and stable, one concrete benefit of final-by-default.

Practical effects.

  • Mocking: Mockito could not mock final classes in tests until mockito-inline (default in Mockito 5); MockK mocks final classes. Teams used to use the kotlin-allopen plugin for Spring, and for Android tests.
  • Frameworks that need open: Spring proxies, Room @Dao abstract classes (declared abstract), Hilt/Dagger generated subclasses (abstract class modules), Android base classes (Fragment, ViewModel, RecyclerView.Adapter are open/abstract on purpose).
  • Your domain models (Order, User) should usually remain final data classes.

Real-life picture. A sealed vault door versus a door with a "please come in" sign: you must consciously write the invitation before anyone can change what is behind it.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing Kotlin classes are open like Java's.
  • Overriding a property without realising the getter and backing field can diverge.
  • Forgetting final override to stop a chain.

notes.title: Interfaces with bodies and abstract classes
notes.html:
The idea. A Kotlin interface can contain method bodies and abstract properties. An abstract class can additionally hold state (backing fields) and a constructor.

interface abstract class
Fields with state no (only abstract or getter-based properties) yes
Constructor / init no yes
Multiple per class yes one
Method bodies yes (default methods) yes
Pick when describing a capability ("can be clicked", Closeable) sharing state and partial implementation (Adapter, Worker)

How default method bodies compile.

Before Kotlin 2.2 (default -Xjvm-default=disable; the modes all / all-compatibility could be chosen), the body lived in a nested synthetic class:

public interface Greeter {
    String name();
    String greet();                                    // abstract in the interface itself
    public static final class DefaultImpls {
        public static String greet(Greeter $this) { return "Hi " + $this.name(); }
    }
}
public final class Impl implements Greeter {
    public String name() { return "A"; }
    public String greet() { return Greeter.DefaultImpls.greet(this); }   // generated bridge
}

Kotlin 2.2. The flag was renamed -jvm-default, now with modes enable (the new default), no-compatibility, disable. In enable, default bodies compile to real JVM default methods in the interface, and DefaultImpls is still generated for binary compatibility with code compiled the old way. no-compatibility drops DefaultImpls. The annotation @JvmDefaultWithCompatibility and @JvmDefaultWithoutCompatibility tune individual interfaces. Real JVM defaults require JVM target 1.8 or higher (Android handles them with D8 desugaring below API 24; confirm in AGP docs). Check the release notes for your exact version.

Industry usage. Comparable, Iterable, Compose's Modifier.Element, Lifecycle observers (DefaultLifecycleObserver is an interface with empty default methods, exactly this feature), Room Dao interfaces with @Transaction default methods (needs -Xjvm-default configuration or abstract classes).

Real-life picture. An interface is a driver's licence category ("may drive trucks"): it says what you may do, and you may hold several. An abstract class is a family business you inherit: you get the building and the equipment (state), but only one family at a time.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying interfaces cannot have implementations (Java 7 view).
  • Forgetting that an interface cannot hold a backing field (val x = 1 is not allowed; only val x get() = 1).
  • Mixing up DefaultImpls (old) with JVM default (new, 2.2 default).

notes.title: Interface default methods and binary compatibility
notes.html:
The incident pattern. A published SDK adds a new method with a default body to a public interface. It is source-compatible and the team ships a minor version. Customer apps that compiled earlier crash in production: java.lang.AbstractMethodError: abstract method "void Listener.onRetry()", usually from classes that implement the interface and were compiled before the change, or from Java code.

Why (pre-2.2 DefaultImpls mode). The implementing class was compiled with generated bridges for the methods it knew about. A newly added default method has no bridge in the old compiled class, so the JVM finds the interface method abstract (the real body is in DefaultImpls) and throws on the first call. Recompiling the consumer fixes it, but consumers who just update the dependency (Gradle resolves a newer version transitively, e.g. one library updates another) do not recompile.

How to avoid it.

  1. Treat "add a method to a public interface" as binary-breaking unless you know the compile mode. Use -jvm-default=enable (Kotlin 2.2 default) or -Xjvm-default=all-compatibility for libraries (generating both a JVM default method and DefaultImpls), and mark the interface with @JvmDefaultWithCompatibility where needed.
  2. Run kotlinx.binary-compatibility-validator (BCV) or Metalava in CI to diff the public API (.api dump) and fail the build on accidental changes.
  3. Prefer an abstract base class (BaseListener with empty open methods) in SDKs consumed by Java callers, or an additional interface for the new method (ListenerV2 : Listener).
  4. Document minimum compatible versions; use semantic versioning with the major version bumped for incompatible changes.

Post-incident review points. What was shipped (minor with an interface change), why CI did not catch it (no API dump check), how the crash looks in Crashlytics (AbstractMethodError in the customer's class, not in yours), how it was mitigated (hotfix, pinned versions, Revert), and the permanent fix (BCV plus compile-mode setting plus a consumer-compat test that compiles against the old version and runs against the new).

Real-life picture. A phone charger standard adds a new pin: new phones have it built-in, old phones lack it. New chargers that depend on the pin leave old phones with a dead cable; shipping a compatibility tip fixes it.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing source compatibility implies binary compatibility.
  • Calling it a Gradle problem instead of a compile-mode problem.
  • Assuming the Kotlin 2.2 default helps already-compiled consumer binaries.

notes.title: Visibility modifiers
notes.html:
Four levels.

Modifier Who can see it
public (default) everyone
internal anything in the same module (one Gradle module/source set compiled together)
protected the class and its subclasses only (members only; not top-level)
private inside the class (members) or inside the file (top-level declarations)

Differences from Java.

  • No package-private level. internal is module-wide, usually bigger than a package. The nearest Java equivalent for "default" does not exist.
  • Kotlin protected does not give access to other classes in the same package, unlike Java.
  • A top-level private fun/class is visible in the whole file, handy for hidden helpers.
  • An outer class cannot see the private members of its nested/inner classes (Java allows it).
  • Default is public, not package-private.
  • A declaration cannot expose a less visible type in its signature ("exposes its private return type") because callers could not use it.
  • Constructors, property accessors (private set), and local classes follow the same keywords; private set on a var is the idiom for controlled mutation.

Bytecode mapping. public = ACC_PUBLIC, private = private (nested access via synthetic access$ bridges or nest mates), protected = protected, internal = public with mangling for members (next section).

Industry usage. Large modularised apps (Airbnb, Uber, Slack) keep each feature module's public surface to a few interfaces and entry points, everything else internal, which keeps incremental builds fast and prevents cross-feature coupling. Libraries use explicit API mode (kotlin { explicitApi() }) so every public declaration has an explicit modifier.

Real-life picture. public is the shop's front door; internal is "staff only" for anyone employed by the company in that building; protected is "family only"; private is your bedroom.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming protected includes the package.
  • Expecting private top-level declarations to be class-private rather than file-private.
  • Exposing a private type in a public API.

notes.title: How internal works on the JVM
notes.html:
The idea. The JVM has no concept of "module" at this level, so internal is enforced by the Kotlin compiler, not the runtime.

Bytecode.

  • An internal class compiles to a normal public class (no mangling).
  • An internal member function or property accessor compiles to a public method whose name is mangled with the module name: fun sync() in module app becomes sync$app_release() (the suffix is the module name, including the build variant for Android).
public final void sync$app_release() { ... }     // internal fun sync()

Kotlin code in another module is blocked at compile time. Java code and reflection can call the mangled name freely.

Consequences.

  • It is a guard against accidental use, not a security boundary. Anyone can call Foo.sync$app_release() from Java.
  • Renaming a Gradle module or changing variants changes mangled names: Java callers, reflection, and mocking libraries by name break, and so can serialised references.
  • Tests: the test source set of the same module is a "friend" and can see internal; other modules need -Xfriend-paths (or test fixtures) to see it.
  • inline public functions cannot call internal code directly (the inlined body would run in other modules). Use @PublishedApi internal fun to make it callable from a public inline function (it stays binary-visible).
  • Android libraries: internal is not hidden from Java consumers or from the AAR's API surface; use @RestrictTo(LIBRARY_GROUP) so lint warns Java users, and R8 consumer rules or separate artifacts for real hiding. Explicit API mode makes you decide on every declaration.
  • In a multi-module Android app, internal ends at the module boundary: a data module cannot hide a class from the app module unless the app module does not depend on it (use Gradle implementation rather than api to reduce leakage).

Industry usage. Jetpack libraries mark implementation details internal or @RestrictTo; Room-generated code uses internal-like constructs; Compose's public API surface is guarded by API-dump files (BCV) so internal leaks are visible.

Real-life picture. A "staff only" sign on an unlocked door. Honest visitors respect it; anyone who deliberately walks in is not stopped, but they will find the room has been renamed after each renovation.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling internal a security feature.
  • Forgetting @PublishedApi for internal helpers used by public inline functions.
  • Reflection-based DI or serialisation hitting mangled names after a module rename.

notes.title: Nested versus inner classes
notes.html:
The idea. A class declared inside another class is nested by default: a normal class that merely lives in the outer class's namespace and does not know the outer object exists. Add the keyword inner and each instance gets a hidden reference to an instance of the outer class.

class Screen {
    val title = "Home"
    class Nested { fun x() = 1 }                 // no access to 'title'
    inner class Inner { fun t() = title }        // can use title, holds a Screen
}
val n = Screen.Nested()          // no Screen needed
val i = Screen().Inner()         // needs a Screen instance

Bytecode. Nested is public static final class Screen$Nested (like Java's static nested class). Inner is Screen$Inner with a synthetic final field this$0 of type Screen, set by a constructor parameter. this@Screen inside Inner compiles to this$0. Note: Kotlin's defaults are the opposite of Java, where a plain nested class is inner and you must write static.

Cost. One reference field (4 or 8 bytes) per inner instance, plus the lifetime coupling: the outer object cannot be garbage collected while any inner instance is reachable.

Where inner is the right tool. Genuinely needing outer state: an iterator over the outer collection, ViewHolder-like helpers that read adapter state, a builder that reads the owner. Everything else should be nested.

Real-life picture. A nested class is a neighbour with their own house. An inner class is a lodger who lives in your house and keeps a key. As long as the lodger exists, your house cannot be demolished.

Common interview traps.

  • Swapping the Java and Kotlin defaults.
  • Saying inner only affects syntax: it adds a field and retains the outer.
  • Trying to instantiate Outer.Inner() without an outer instance.

notes.title: The inner class leak bug
notes.html:
The scenario (spot-the-bug). A screen has an inner Handler/Runnable/Thread/callback class. The Activity is rotated or finished, but the background work is still queued, so the inner object keeps this$0 pointing at the destroyed Activity.

class FeedActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    inner class Poller : Thread() {                 // implicit this$0 = FeedActivity
        override fun run() { while (true) { refresh(); Thread.sleep(30_000) } }
    }
    override fun onCreate(b: Bundle?) { super.onCreate(b); Poller().start() }
}

Every rotation creates a new Activity and a new, never-ending Poller. After a few rotations: several full Activities with all their views and bitmaps retained, heap growth, OutOfMemoryError, ANR from GC pressure. LeakCanary shows:

GC ROOT Thread FeedActivity$Poller (named 'Thread-3')
 -> FeedActivity$Poller.this$0
 -> FeedActivity (leaking: Activity#mDestroyed = true)

Fixes.

  1. Use a nested (non-inner) class and pass only what is needed, or a WeakReference to a narrow callback.
  2. Prefer structured concurrency: lifecycleScope.launch { repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) { ... } }: the coroutine dies with the lifecycle.
  3. Cancel work in onDestroy/onStop; remove Handler messages (removeCallbacksAndMessages(null)).
  4. Don't register inner/anonymous listeners on long-lived objects (singletons, Application) without removal.
  5. Run LeakCanary in debug builds; look for this$0, val$ (captured locals), and arg$1 in the leak trace.

Also leaking: lambdas and anonymous objects. A lambda that calls an Activity method captures this; an object : Runnable created in a member function holds this$0. A non-capturing lambda captures nothing and is safe.

Real-life picture. A contractor's badge that opens your house: when you move out, the contractor still holds the key and the house cannot be given to someone else.

Common interview traps.

  • Using WeakReference but still holding a strong reference elsewhere.
  • Believing Kotlin lambdas always leak: only capturing ones.
  • Fixing the symptom with onDestroy flags rather than lifecycle-aware scopes.

notes.title: Anonymous objects and what they capture
notes.html:
The idea. object : Runnable { override fun run() { ... } } creates a one-off instance of an unnamed class that implements or extends something. It is an expression, not a declaration.

val listener = object : View.OnClickListener {
    var clicks = 0
    override fun onClick(v: View) { clicks++; counter++ }    // can mutate captured 'counter'
}

Facts.

  • Captures the outer this when it uses outer members and is created inside a member function (field this$0). Same leak risk as inner classes. In a top-level function or if it uses only locals, no outer reference.
  • Captures locals, even mutable ones. Kotlin wraps a captured var in a Ref.IntRef / Ref.ObjectRef (a heap box), unlike Java's effectively-final rule. Each captured mutable var costs a small allocation and visibility is not synchronised across threads.
  • Compile-time type. If a private member or a local variable holds it, you can use the object's extra members (listener.clicks works); if a public property or function returns it, the declared type becomes the supertype (or Any), and extra members vanish:
private fun make() = object { val x = 1 }    // type is the anonymous type: make().x compiles
fun makePublic() = object { val x = 1 }      // public: inferred as Any, make().x does NOT compile
  • Implements multiple supertypes: object : A(), B { ... }.
  • SAM / lambda difference. Runnable { ... } (SAM-converted lambda) compiles to a lambda (invokedynamic on newer Kotlin targets, or a generated class), and a non-capturing one is a cached singleton; object : Runnable always allocates a new instance (identity matters for removeCallbacks: keep the reference).
  • Class names appear in stack traces as FeedActivity$onCreate$1.

Industry usage. RecyclerView.OnScrollListener, Callbacks of Retrofit/Glide, ViewTreeObserver.OnGlobalLayoutListener, ActivityResultCallback, object : DiffUtil.ItemCallback<Item>().

Real-life picture. A temporary employee hired for one job with a badge that opens the building: convenient, but the badge (outer reference) must be returned when the job ends.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming an object expression is a singleton (a new instance every time the expression runs).
  • Leaking an Activity through an anonymous listener on a global.
  • Losing extra members by returning an anonymous object from a public function.

notes.title: Constructors and initialization order
notes.html:
The idea. Creating an object runs code in a strict order, and reading something before its turn gives you its default value (0, false, null), even if the type says non-null.

Order.

  1. Arguments are evaluated; for a secondary constructor, its delegation call (: this(...) / : super(...)) runs first.
  2. The superclass constructor runs fully (including its property initialisers and init blocks) before anything in the subclass.
  3. In the subclass: property initialisers and init blocks run in the exact order they appear in the source, top to bottom, interleaved.
  4. The body of a secondary constructor runs last.
class User(val id: Long, name: String) {            // 'name' is a plain parameter, usable in initialisers
    val upper = name.uppercase()                    // 1
    init { println("init 1: $upper") }              // 2
    val len = upper.length                          // 3
    init { println("init 2: $len") }                // 4
    constructor(id: Long) : this(id, "anon") { println("secondary body") }   // 5
}

Primary vs secondary. The primary constructor sits in the class header; parameters with val/var become properties. A class with a primary constructor requires every secondary constructor to delegate to it (: this(...), directly or indirectly). A class with no primary constructor lets secondary constructors call super(...). Default arguments replace most overloads; @JvmOverloads generates the Java overloads, which matters for custom Views (View(context), View(context, attrs), View(context, attrs, defStyle)).

Bytecode. All property initialisers and init blocks are copied into the constructor (<init>) in source order, after the super(...) call. Properties with default values and no initialiser still get a default value from the JVM allocation (zeroed memory).

Validation. init { require(age >= 0) { "age must be non-negative" } } is the normal place to guard; an exception thrown there aborts construction (no partially built object escapes).

Industry usage. ViewModels with init { load() } (reads properties declared above it!), custom Views using @JvmOverloads constructor, Room entities with default values.

Real-life picture. Building a house: the foundation (parent class) is poured first, then your floors (properties), then furniture (init blocks), and finally the decorating team (secondary body). Using the kitchen before its turn means no plumbing yet.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing all properties are initialised before any init block.
  • Forgetting that parent-class code runs before child fields exist.
  • Expecting the secondary constructor body to run before init blocks.

notes.title: Init order bug inside one class
notes.html:
The scenario (spot-the-bug).

class ProfileViewModel(private val repo: Repo) : ViewModel() {
    init { load() }                                   // runs here, at position 1
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(State())    // initialised AFTER init, so still null in load()
    fun load() { viewModelScope.launch { _state.value = State(repo.get()) } }
}

load() runs from the first init block while _state is still null: the coroutine starts on Dispatchers.Main.immediate, hits _state.value = ... and crashes with NullPointerException: Attempt to invoke virtual method ... StateFlow.setValue() on a null object reference, or with IllegalStateException in intrinsics checks. With a dispatcher that delays the coroutine it may "work in testing" and fail only on fast devices (race).

Rule. An init block (or property initialiser) sees only the properties declared above it. Declared-below properties read as 0/false/null.

Fixes.

  1. Move init { load() } below the properties it uses (the simplest, and many style guides put init last).
  2. Initialise properties inline and call load() from a lifecycle hook or onStart (LaunchedEffect, stateIn(... SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed)).
  3. Prefer cold flows (stateIn, flow {}) so nothing starts until collected.
  4. Enable the Kotlin inspection "Property used before initialisation"; unit-test the ViewModel in runTest with a test dispatcher.

Real-life picture. A cook who starts cooking from the recipe before the shopping bag has been unpacked: the recipe steps are right, but the ingredients are not on the counter yet.

Common interview traps.

  • Declaring init at the top and the state fields below.
  • Assuming the compiler rejects this (it often only warns for direct reads, not through function calls).
  • "Works on emulator, fails on device": a timing-dependent coroutine masks the order bug.

notes.title: Calling open members during construction
notes.html:
The idea. When a base-class constructor calls an open function, the subclass override runs before the subclass's own properties are initialised. Non-null properties can be null, Int can be 0. This is one of the holes in Kotlin's null safety.

open class Base {
    init { println("Base init"); describe() }
    open fun describe() = println("Base")
}
class Derived : Base() {
    private val name = "Derived"                       // set AFTER Base's init
    init { println("Derived init, name=$name") }
    override fun describe() = println("name=$name")    // prints name=null from Base's init
}
Derived()   // Base init / name=null / Derived init, name=Derived

Decompiled: Derived.<init> calls Base.<init>() first; Base.<init> calls this.describe() (virtual) which reads Derived.name (still null) before this.name = "Derived" executes.

Production incident pattern. A base BaseView/BasePresenter calls an abstract setup() or layoutId() in its constructor; the subclass override reads a subclass val (a LayoutInflater, an adapter, a lateinit not yet set) and crashes with NPE, or silently uses 0. It appears after someone refactors a hard-coded value into a field, or after adding a subclass property. Crashlytics shows an NPE inside an override, called from the base class constructor in the stack trace.

Fixes.

  • Never call open/abstract functions or access open properties in a constructor or init (the IDE warns "Calling non-final function in constructor").
  • Make helpers private or final, pass needed values as constructor parameters, or use a two-step pattern (constructor builds; a factory or start() calls the hook after construction).
  • Use composition: a strategy object passed in, instead of an overridable method.
  • Compose ViewModel base classes: expose abstract val only after construction (use by lazy).

Related: lateinit in subclasses and Java frameworks that call overridable methods from constructors (e.g. old View constructors calling onFinishInflate).

Real-life picture. A builder whose general contractor starts the plumbing job in a flat by asking the sub-contractor to "fit the tap", before the sub-contractor has installed the sink.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing non-null types guarantee a value in all code paths.
  • Making the property lateinit to silence the warning (still crashes).
  • Forgetting that abstract val is also virtual and has the same problem.

notes.title: Value classes: the basics
notes.html:
The idea. Many types are "just a number or a string" underneath, but mean very different things: UserId, OrderId, Email, Millis, Dp. Mixing them up compiles fine with plain Long/String. A value class wraps one value to give it a distinct type at compile time, and usually costs nothing at runtime because the wrapper is erased.

@JvmInline
value class UserId(val value: Long)
@JvmInline
value class OrderId(val value: Long)

fun load(order: OrderId, user: UserId) { ... }
load(UserId(1), OrderId(2))        // compile error: the types are swapped

Rules. @JvmInline value class with exactly one val property in the primary constructor; the class is final; it can have functions, computed properties, init blocks (1.9+), can implement interfaces; no backing fields except the one value; no identity (do not use ===).

Versus alternatives.

typealias UserId = Long data class UserId(val v: Long) value class UserId(val v: Long)
New type for the compiler no (just a name) yes yes
Runtime object none (a Long) always an object (16+ bytes) none when used as itself (a long)
Prevents swapped arguments no yes yes
equals/hashCode/toString Long's generated generated (on the value)
copy, destructuring n/a yes no
Identity n/a yes no

Decompiled use. UserId(5) as an argument becomes the primitive long 5; the class UserId exists in bytecode with static helpers (constructor-impl, equals-impl, hashCode-impl, toString-impl, box-impl, unbox-impl).

Industry examples. Compose's Dp, Color, Offset, IntSize, TextUnit (value classes over Float/Long, which is how Compose avoids allocating objects during layout/draw), kotlin.time.Duration (a Long), kotlin.Result, and typed ids in domain layers of banking and e-commerce apps. kotlinx.serialization supports inline value classes.

Real-life picture. A cheque, cash and a gift card are all "money", but a shop that needs cash will refuse a gift card. A value class puts the right label on each, without making you carry an extra box.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling a value class "a data class without allocation": no copy, no identity, one field only.
  • Using typealias and expecting type safety.
  • Expecting value class to be free everywhere (see boxing).

notes.title: When value classes box
notes.html:
The idea. The compiler inlines a value class to its underlying value wherever the static type is the value class itself. When the value is used as something else, it must become a real object ("box") because the other type does not know about the erasure.

Boxing happens when the value class is used as:

  • a generic type argument: List<UserId>, Set<UserId>, Map<UserId, X>, Result<UserId>, Flow<UserId>;
  • Any, or an interface it implements (val x: Comparable<UserId> = id);
  • a nullable type when the underlying type is a primitive or a nullable type: UserId? over Long boxes (the null needs a reference). For a non-null reference underlying type (value class Email(val s: String)), Email? is represented as String? and does not box;
  • a function type or lambda parameter/return ((UserId) -> Unit is Function1<UserId, Unit>), unless the function is inline;
  • vararg/arrays: Array<UserId> holds boxes (LongArray-like inline arrays are not available);
  • lateinit/delegate and reflection paths.

Cost. Each boxed instance is an object: roughly 16 bytes for a Long-backed box (header + 8 bytes, aligned), box-impl on the way in, unbox-impl on the way out. A List<UserId> of a million elements is a million small objects plus an array of references, roughly the same as List<Long>, so the gain over List<Long> is type safety, not memory.

Where it bites. Hot paths (RecyclerView bind, Compose LazyColumn item lambdas with keys, per-frame draw code), large collections, and Map<UserId, T> lookups (hash of the box). Perfetto and the Memory Profiler show allocation counts for UserId.

Mitigation. Convert at the boundary and keep raw LongArray/primitive collections inside tight code, use inline lambdas, avoid nullable value classes in hot structures (use a sentinel UserId(-1)), keep value classes as parameters and locals.

Real-life picture. A parcel that travels naked while it stays in the sorting room, but must be put in a box whenever it goes through the generic conveyor belt.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying value classes never allocate.
  • Forgetting UserId? over Long boxes but over String does not.
  • Measuring only on emulator rather than allocation profiler.

notes.title: Value class name mangling and Java interop
notes.html:
The idea. After inlining, fun load(id: UserId) and fun load(id: Long) would have the same JVM signature load(J)V and clash. To prevent that, the compiler mangles the JVM name of any function whose signature includes a value class: it appends a hyphen and a short hash.

// fun load(id: UserId)       -> load-ABC123xyz(long id)
// fun load(id: Long)         -> load(long id)
// val UserId.display: String -> getDisplay-ABC123xyz(long $this)

The hash is derived from the signature's value-class types, so it is stable for the same signature but differs by parameter types.

What breaks.

  • Java callers cannot call load-ABC123xyz (a hyphen is not legal in Java identifiers; a few tools can) and cannot use UserId at all, only the raw long. A public API consumed from Java should avoid value classes in signatures, or expose a @JvmName("load") alternative function on non-value types (you can use @JvmName on functions that do not conflict).
  • Reflection: Class.getMethod("load") fails; kotlin-reflect handles mangled functions but with more overhead; DI frameworks and mocking libraries that look up methods by name can break (MockK has support, older Mockito does not).
  • Serialisation: kotlinx.serialization supports @Serializable @JvmInline value class by serialising the underlying value; Gson sees a plain field named after the property in the containing class (the inlined primitive) or can mis-handle the value class itself (confirm per version); Moshi reflection/codegen needs a recent version (confirm in docs); Room needs @TypeConverter (value-class support in Room is limited, confirm for your version); Parcelable via @Parcelize works for value-class properties in recent versions.
  • Binary compatibility: changing a parameter type from Long to UserId in a published library renames the JVM method. Old binaries break (NoSuchMethodError). Plan the migration with @Deprecated keep-alive overloads.
  • Interfaces and overriding behave normally but mangling applies to generated bridge methods; R8 keeps names per rules.

Industry usage. Compose's public API exposes Dp/Color; Java users of Compose are rare, which is why Google can use mangled value classes freely. A public Android SDK for Java users (payments, ads) usually avoids them.

Real-life picture. Two keys that look identical to the lock after the plating is removed; to avoid mixing them up, the locksmith engraves a tiny serial on each. Only the Kotlin staff can read the engraving.

Common interview traps.

  • Offering a value class in the public API of a Java-first SDK.
  • Using reflection or mocks by method name against a function that takes a value class.
  • Changing Long to a value class in a published signature and calling it "source compatible".

notes.title: Value class boxing in hot paths
notes.html:
The scenario. A team replaces Long ids with value class ProductId(val v: Long) across a catalogue app. After the release, scroll jank rises on low-end phones and the GC graph in Perfetto shows many short collections. The Memory Profiler allocation view lists hundreds of thousands of ProductId allocations per screen.

Why. Typical offenders:

  • LazyColumn(items, key = { it.id }) where the key lambda returns a ProductId: the key type is generic (Any), so each item boxes.
  • Map<ProductId, Product> caches and Set<ProductId> for selection; every lookup boxes the key and hashes the box.
  • List<ProductId> pipelines (map, filter, groupBy) on thousands of ids.
  • StateFlow<ProductId?> or Flow<ProductId> in hot streams.
  • Pair<ProductId, Int> results.

Cost/perf optimisation plan.

  1. Measure: Android Studio allocation tracker or Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric before and after; check box-impl call counts in method traces.
  2. Keep value classes at API edges (function parameters, locals, class fields: a ProductId field in a class is stored as a long, no box).
  3. Inside hot loops, work on primitives: LongArray, LongSparseArray, androidx.collection.LongObjectMap/MutableLongSet (primitive-specialised collections), and convert once with .value.
  4. Use inline higher-order functions (forEach, any) which inline lambdas and avoid boxing; avoid Sequence lambdas on value-class types in hot code.
  5. For Compose keys, use it.id.value (a Long, which still boxes in key but is cached for small values; or use Long-keyed stable LazyListScope.items(key = ...)).
  6. Avoid nullable value classes (ProductId?) in hot data; use a sentinel.
  7. Accept boxing when counts are small: a few hundred boxes per screen are noise.

Trade-off summary. Value classes remove the field-and-argument allocations but not the generic-container ones. If most uses are in collections, a plain Long plus naming discipline, or a regular data class (honest allocation), may be simpler.

Real-life picture. Parcels travel loose inside the warehouse but go into a box every time they ride the generic conveyor belt; if everything rides the belt all day, the "no box" saving disappears and you only paid the extra paperwork.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming "zero cost" without profiling.
  • Replacing Long with value classes inside primitive-specialised collections and boxing everything again.
  • Forgetting that Comparable/Map.Entry interface use also boxes.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Choosing a closed type. Enum: fixed same-shape instances. Sealed class: fixed subtypes with different data and a shared parent state. Sealed interface: same, with freedom to extend other classes. All allow exhaustive when without else; a missing case is a compile error.

Sealed rules. Direct subclasses in the same package and same module (files may differ since 1.5); indirect subclasses anywhere; constructors protected; Java cannot extend. Across modules or precompiled SDKs a stale when throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException; for server-driven data add an Unknown case and tolerant deserialisation (Moshi withDefaultValue, kotlinx.serialization polymorphicDefaultDeserializer).

Inheritance. Final by default; open is a promise; abstract members are open; override is open unless final override. Interfaces carry bodies (DefaultImpls before Kotlin 2.2, real JVM defaults with -jvm-default=enable since 2.2); adding a default method to a published interface can cause AbstractMethodError: use compatibility modes and a binary-compatibility validator.

Visibility. public, internal (module), protected (subclasses only), private (class or file). internal is public bytecode with mangled member names (foo$app_release): a compile-time guard, not a wall; use @PublishedApi for inline helpers and @RestrictTo for Java consumers.

Nested, inner, anonymous. Nested has no outer reference; inner and capturing anonymous objects hold this$0, the cause of many Activity leaks (LeakCanary trace). Anonymous objects capture mutable locals through Ref boxes and lose extra members when returned from public APIs.

Initialization order. Superclass first, then properties and init blocks in source order, then the secondary constructor body. Properties declared below an init are not ready; open members called from constructors see uninitialised subclass state (null or 0 even for non-null types).

Value classes. @JvmInline value class gives a distinct compile-time type with no wrapper while used as itself. It boxes as a generic argument, Any/interface, nullable-over-primitive, in function types, and in arrays. Functions taking them are name-mangled (load-<hash>), which hurts Java, reflection, and library binary compatibility; keep them out of hot collections and Java-facing APIs.

Interview one-liners.

  • "Sealed means the compiler knows the full list, so a missing case is a compile error, unless it was compiled separately."
  • "Kotlin classes are final by default: open is a promise."
  • "internal is mangled public: a guard, not a wall."
  • "An inner class is a lodger holding a key to your Activity."
  • "Never call an open function from a constructor; below-declared properties are still null."
  • "Value classes are free until you put them in a List."

questions.subtopic: Sealed class vs sealed interface vs enum
questions.promptHtml: When would you use an enum, a sealed class, or a sealed interface? Give me a concrete example of each.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the base question for modeling UI state and results in Kotlin. They want to hear about instance shape and identity, not just "sealed is a better enum".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I use an enum when every case has the same shape and exactly one instance, like SortOrder.ASC/DESC. I use a sealed type when the cases carry different data, like Loading, Success(items) and Error(throwable), because each subtype can be a data class, an object or a regular class with its own properties. Between the two sealed kinds, I default to a sealed interface. A sealed class only earns its place when the cases share constructor state or a common implementation. A sealed interface also lets one type belong to several hierarchies, and an enum can implement one.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Think of it as a closed set of either values or types:

enum class sealed class sealed interface
What is closed the set of instances the set of direct subtypes the set of direct subtypes
Instances per case exactly one, created at class init as many as you construct (or one if object) same as sealed class
Per-case data shape same constructor for all constants different per subtype different per subtype
Shared state / constructor yes (enum constructor) yes (abstract class, protected/private ctor) no state, only abstract members and default methods
Subtype can extend another class n/a no, it already extends the sealed class yes
Type in multiple hierarchies no no (single inheritance) yes
Built-in listing entries (Kotlin 1.9+), valueOf none without reflection (sealedSubclasses needs kotlin-reflect) same
Serialization by name, EnumMap, ordinal yes no no

How they compile:

  • An enum is a final class with one static final field per constant, all created when the class initializes.
  • A sealed class is an abstract class whose constructor Kotlin won't let anyone outside the allowed package/module call.
  • A sealed interface is a plain JVM interface. The "sealed" part is enforced by the Kotlin compiler, plus Kotlin metadata that lists the subclasses so when can be checked for exhaustiveness.

Rules of thumb:

  • Finite, same-shape, needs ordering, persistence by name, or a Map key: enum.
  • Variant data (state machines, results, navigation destinations, UI events): sealed interface.
  • Variants that all need, say, a timestamp stored in a constructor, or a template method: sealed class.
  • Mixing: an enum can implement a sealed interface. That gives you ErrorType.NETWORK, ErrorType.DISK as constants plus ValidationError(field) as a data class, all under one sealed interface AppError.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
enum class SortOrder { ASC, DESC }                       // same shape, singletons

sealed interface UiState {
    data object Loading : UiState
    data class Success(val items: List<Item>) : UiState
    data class Error(val cause: Throwable) : UiState
}

sealed class Message(val sentAt: Long) {                 // shared constructor state
    class Text(sentAt: Long, val body: String) : Message(sentAt)
    class Image(sentAt: Long, val url: String) : Message(sentAt)
}

sealed interface AppError
enum class SystemError : AppError { NETWORK, DISK }      // enum implementing sealed interface
data class ValidationError(val field: String) : AppError

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using an enum and then adding a nullable payload: Any? to fake per-case data. That's the signal it should be sealed.
  • Using a sealed class with no shared state, which forces every subtype to waste its one superclass slot.
  • Writing class Loading : UiState() instead of object/data object. Every emission allocates and == fails, so distinctUntilChanged and StateFlow equality stop deduplicating.
  • Assuming a sealed type can be iterated like entries. It can't without reflection.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can an enum extend a sealed class? → No. An enum already extends kotlin.Enum, but it can implement a sealed interface.
  2. Which one is cheaper at runtime? → Enum constants and object subtypes are allocated once. Data-class subtypes allocate per instance. when over an enum compiles to a tableswitch on the ordinal (via a mapping array). when over sealed is checks compiles to an instanceof chain. Both are negligible except in very hot loops.
  3. How would you persist a sealed hierarchy? → Not by class name, which breaks under R8 renaming and refactors. Use an explicit discriminator, for example @SerialName with kotlinx.serialization, or map to an enum or string at the storage boundary.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "sealed classes are like enums that can hold data." The senior answer talks about closing a set of values vs a set of types, single vs multiple inheritance, enums implementing sealed interfaces, the equality impact of object vs class subtypes on StateFlow, and persistence and R8 concerns.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team modeled Loading as class Loading : UiState(). Every refresh emitted a new non-equal instance, so distinctUntilChanged never filtered it and the shimmer animation restarted on every poll.

questions.subtopic: final by default, open, abstract, override
questions.promptHtml: Why are Kotlin classes and members final by default? How do open, abstract and override interact?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you understand inheritance as an API commitment, and whether you know the practical fallout for testing and frameworks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Kotlin follows the "design for inheritance or prohibit it" rule. Every class and member is final unless you mark it open, so a subclass can't depend on internals you never promised to keep stable. abstract implies open and has no implementation. An override is itself open unless you write final override. The cost shows up with tools that need subclassing, like mocking libraries and some frameworks. In practice that's solved with Mockito's inline mock maker or MockK, or with the all-open compiler plugin. I don't solve it by sprinkling open everywhere.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The fragile base class problem. If a base class calls its own overridable method internally (for example, addAll calls add), a subclass overriding add now depends on that internal call pattern. If the base changes that pattern, the subclass silently breaks. Final by default means every extension point is a deliberate decision.
  • Bytecode. Kotlin classes compile to public final class and members to final methods unless marked open. Final methods are also easier for R8 and ART to inline and devirtualize, though that's a side benefit, not the reason.
  • The modifier matrix:
Declaration Overridable? Has body?
fun f() in a class no (final) yes
open fun f() yes yes
abstract fun f() must be no
override fun f() yes, still open yes
final override fun f() no yes
member of an interface yes (open by default) optional
  • An open member inside a final class gets a compiler warning, because nothing can ever override it.
  • An abstract class can override an open member with an abstract one, which forces subclasses to reimplement it.
  • The tooling impact:
    • Mockito before version 5 could not mock final classes without mockito-inline. Mockito 5 made the inline mock maker the default on the JVM.
    • MockK mocks finals via instrumentation.
    • For Android instrumented tests, mocking finals needs dexmaker-mockito-inline, which has an API-level floor (I believe API 28+, so verify for your setup).
    • Frameworks that proxy classes, like Spring, use the all-open / kotlin-spring plugin. Android rarely needs this.
    • The better fix is usually depending on an interface and passing a fake.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
abstract class Repository {
    abstract suspend fun load(): List<Item>        // must override
    open fun cacheKey(): String = "repo"            // may override
    fun log(msg: String) = println("[${cacheKey()}] $msg")   // final
}

open class UserRepository : Repository() {
    override suspend fun load(): List<Item> = emptyList()
    final override fun cacheKey() = "users"          // subclasses of UserRepository can't change it
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Marking classes open only so tests can mock them. That widens the production API for a test-only need.
  • Forgetting that an override stays open, which lets a third level of inheritance change behavior you thought was fixed.
  • Calling an open method from a constructor or init block. The subclass override runs before the subclass's fields are initialized (see A1-Q071).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Are interface members final? → No. Interface members are implicitly open. You can't mark them final.
  2. Can a data class be open? → No. Data classes are always final (see K2a), but they can extend an open class or implement interfaces.
  3. In a library, what does making a class open commit you to? → Every protected and open member, and the order in which your code calls them internally, become part of the API. Changing them is a breaking change, even if no signature changes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "Kotlin is final by default; add open to extend." The senior answer explains the fragile base class problem, that override stays open, that self-calls become API, and that mocking pressure is solved with inline mock makers or interfaces rather than by opening production classes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A shared BaseFragment was made fully open so a test could mock it. Feature teams then overrode onViewCreated hooks inconsistently. A later refactor of the base call order broke six screens with no compile error.

questions.promptHtml: Explain Kotlin's visibility modifiers. How do they differ from Java's, especially protected and the default?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Developers coming from Java get the defaults and protected wrong. It also shows whether you understand module boundaries as an architecture tool.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Kotlin has four modifiers: public (the default), internal (visible inside the same compilation module), protected (visible in the class and its subclasses only, with no package access unlike Java), and private. private on a class member means that class only. private on a top-level declaration means that file only. Kotlin has no package-private. internal replaces that idea at the module level, which in Android means a Gradle module.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Modifier Top-level declaration Class member Java equivalent / bytecode
public (default) everywhere everywhere the class is visible public
internal same module same module compiled as public; member names are mangled (see A1-Q068)
protected not allowed class + subclasses (no package access) protected in bytecode, so Java in the same package can still call it
private same file the declaring class only private; top-level ones live in the FileNameKt facade class

Points that trip people up:

  • No package-private. Java's default visibility doesn't exist in Kotlin. Same package means nothing for access. Packages are just namespaces.
  • An outer class can't see an inner class's private members. This is the reverse of Java, where an enclosing class can touch its nested classes' privates. A nested or inner class can see its outer class's privates.
  • Overrides inherit visibility. If you don't write a modifier on an override, it keeps the overridden member's visibility (a protected override stays protected). You can widen it explicitly, but never narrow it.
  • Private constructors. class Foo private constructor() is the factory pattern. Sealed class constructors are protected by default and can only be protected or private.
  • Getter and setter visibility. var count: Int = 0; private set exposes a read-only property publicly. That's the idiom for mutable-inside, read-only-outside state (the backing-property pattern is in K6).
  • "Exposes its private-in-file type" errors. A public function can't take or return a type that is internal or private. The compiler enforces that the effective visibility of a signature is no wider than its types.
  • Synthetic accessors. When a lambda or nested class touches a private member of its outer class, older compilers generate access$... static methods. They add method count but are rarely a real concern with R8.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// File: Session.kt
private const val PREFS = "session"          // visible only in Session.kt

internal class TokenStore                     // visible across the :auth module only

class SessionManager internal constructor(    // public type, module-only construction
    private val store: TokenStore
) {
    var userId: String? = null
        private set                           // public read, private write

    protected fun hook() {}                   // warning: protected in final class is effectively private
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting protected to give same-package access, like Java. It doesn't in Kotlin source, although Java callers in the same package can still reach it via bytecode.
  • Treating internal as a security boundary. It's public in bytecode, so Java code and reflection can call it.
  • Making everything public in a library and only later trying to tighten it, which breaks consumers. Turn on explicitApi() mode from day one.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does "module" mean for internal? → One compilation unit: a Gradle source set compilation (main, with test and androidTest treated as friends), a Maven module, or an IntelliJ module.
  2. How do you force library authors to declare visibility? → kotlin { explicitApi() } makes a missing modifier on public API a compile error.
  3. Is private in a file truly private on the JVM? → The facade class member is JVM-private. Java in the same module can't call it, but reflection can, like any private.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer lists the four modifiers. The senior answer explains no package-private, protected without package access, that internal is public in bytecode with name mangling, the outer-can't-see-inner-private rule, effective-visibility rules, and using explicitApi() and module boundaries to enforce architecture.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team relied on internal to hide a debug-only API in an SDK. A Java consumer called the mangled enableDebug$sdk_release() method directly, and it broke when the module was renamed.

questions.promptHtml: What's the difference between a nested class and an inner class in Kotlin? Why does it matter on Android?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the root cause of the classic Activity memory leak, and the default is the opposite of Java's.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In Kotlin, a class declared inside another class is nested by default. That's like a Java static nested class: it holds no reference to the outer instance. Marking it inner gives it a hidden reference to the outer instance, so it can use outer members. That reference is exactly what leaks an Activity or Fragment when an inner-class instance is held by something longer-lived, like a singleton listener list, a Handler message or a background task.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Nested (default): class Outer { class Nested } compiles to Outer$Nested with no outer field. You create it with Outer.Nested(). It can't reach Outer's instance members, only its companion and other statics.
  • Inner: class Outer { inner class In } compiles to Outer$In with a synthetic final Outer this$0 field, set through a hidden constructor parameter. You create it with outer.In(). It can use outer members directly, and this@Outer names the outer instance.
  • Lifetime coupling: the inner instance keeps the outer instance reachable for as long as the inner one is reachable. If the outer is an Activity (about 1–10 MB of view tree, bitmaps and Context), any inner object stored in a static, a singleton, a long-running coroutine or a pending Message keeps the whole screen alive after onDestroy.
Singleton.listeners ──> MainActivity$Listener ──this$0──> MainActivity ──> Window ──> View tree, Bitmaps
 (lives for process)        (inner class)                  (destroyed but unreachable-for-GC: NO)
  • Java contrast: in Java a non-static nested class is inner by default, so Java devs had to remember static. Kotlin flips the default to the safe option, and you have to opt into inner.
  • Anonymous objects and lambdas: they capture the outer this only if the body actually uses an outer member, at least in current Kotlin compilers. If you call showToast() inside a listener, you've captured the Activity. Anonymous objects are covered in A1-Q067.
  • Kotlin vs Java access: a nested class can access the outer class's private members (statics or via an instance you pass in). The outer can't access the nested class's privates.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ProfileActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    // Leaks if registered with a long-lived object and not unregistered
    inner class AvatarListener : ImageLoader.Listener {
        override fun onLoaded(b: Bitmap) { binding.avatar.setImageBitmap(b) }   // uses outer → needs inner
    }

    // Safe by construction: no outer reference
    class DiffCallback : DiffUtil.ItemCallback<Item>() {
        override fun areItemsTheSame(a: Item, b: Item) = a.id == b.id
        override fun areContentsTheSame(a: Item, b: Item) = a == b
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding inner just to silence the "Unresolved reference" error when the nested class uses an outer field, without thinking about lifetime.
  • Assuming WeakReference is the main fix. It works, but the clean fix is lifecycle-scoped registration (unregister in the mirror lifecycle callback) or exposing a Flow collected with repeatOnLifecycle.
  • Holding inner-class ViewHolders or adapters that reference the Fragment, then keeping the adapter in a field across onDestroyView. That leaks the view hierarchy.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you refer to the outer instance from an inner class? → this@Outer. Use it to disambiguate when names shadow.
  2. Can an inner class have a companion object? → No. Inner classes can't declare companion objects or other static-like declarations, because each instance is tied to an outer instance.
  3. How would you prove an inner class is leaking? → A LeakCanary trace showing this$0 pointing at the destroyed Activity (mDestroyed = true), or a heap dump in the Android Studio Memory Profiler filtered by the Activity class with more than one instance after rotations.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "inner can access outer members; nested can't." The senior answer covers the this$0 field, the reachability chain to the Activity, that the default is reversed from Java, that anonymous objects capture only when they use outer members, and lifecycle-scoped registration as the structural fix.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An inner Runnable posted with postDelayed(…, 30_000) on a screen users often left within seconds kept about 40 MB of retained Activities alive across a typical session. It showed up as out-of-memory crashes on 2 GB RAM devices only.

questions.subtopic: Exhaustive when and adding a subclass
questions.promptHtml: How does exhaustive when work with sealed types? What happens when someone adds a new subclass?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Exhaustiveness is the main reason to use sealed types. Seniors know where the guarantee breaks: else branches, statements on older Kotlin versions, expect classes, and library consumers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Because the compiler knows every direct subtype of a sealed type, a when that covers them all needs no else. If someone adds a subtype, every exhaustive when without an else becomes a compile error, which is exactly what I want. Since Kotlin 1.7, that applies to when statements over sealed, enum and Boolean subjects as well as to when expressions. The guarantee disappears the moment someone writes else ->, so I avoid else on sealed subjects in domain code.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Mechanism. Kotlin metadata on the sealed class lists its direct subclasses. In a when (x) with is A, is B or C (an object) branches, the compiler checks that the union covers that list, recursing into sealed subclasses: covering is IOError covers all of IOError's subtypes.
  • Expression vs statement history:
Kotlin version when used as expression when used as statement
< 1.6 must be exhaustive non-exhaustive allowed silently
1.6 must be exhaustive warning for sealed/enum/Boolean
1.7+ must be exhaustive error for sealed/enum/Boolean
  • What compiles under the hood. Branches on a sealed type become an instanceof chain in source order. The compiler still emits a throwing default branch (a NoWhenBranchMatchedException) for the impossible case, for example when a class compiled separately has a subtype the caller never saw.
  • Where the guarantee leaks:
    1. else -> swallows new cases silently. A new UiState.Partial falls into else -> showError().
    2. expect sealed classes in KMP common code need an else, because actual implementations can add platform subtypes.
    3. Binary consumers. If a library adds a subtype and an app is not recompiled (for example, a prebuilt AAR built against the old version), the app's when hits the synthetic throw at runtime. Adding a sealed subtype is source-breaking for consumers on purpose, and binary-dangerous for prebuilt ones.
    4. Data from outside (JSON, DB, server-driven UI) can contain a type the client doesn't know. Exhaustiveness is a compile-time property, not a runtime defense (see A1-Q073).
  • Smart casts inside branches. is Success -> smart-casts the subject, so x.items is directly usable. Guard conditions (is Success if x.items.isEmpty() ->) went stable in Kotlin 2.2. See K8 for the language-feature details.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface PaymentResult {
    data class Success(val receiptId: String) : PaymentResult
    data class Declined(val reason: String) : PaymentResult
    data object Cancelled : PaymentResult
}

fun render(r: PaymentResult): String = when (r) {      // no else → adding a subtype breaks the build here
    is PaymentResult.Success -> "Paid ${r.receiptId}"
    is PaymentResult.Declined -> "Declined: ${r.reason}"
    PaymentResult.Cancelled -> "Cancelled"
}

// Trap: this silently routes any future subtype to "error"
fun renderBad(r: PaymentResult) = when (r) {
    is PaymentResult.Success -> "Paid"
    else -> "Something went wrong"
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding else "for safety", which removes the safety.
  • Using is for a data object. It works, but a plain Cancelled -> (an equality check) reads better and is equivalent for a singleton.
  • Forcing exhaustiveness with a val Any?.exhaustive get() = this extension. That trick was needed before 1.7 for statements and is obsolete now.
  • Believing exhaustiveness protects against unknown server types. It doesn't.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does exhaustiveness work on is checks of an open subclass of a sealed type? → Yes, if you cover the open subclass with is OpenSub, which includes all its descendants. You can't enumerate its descendants individually for exhaustiveness.
  2. What runtime exception fires if an impossible branch is reached? → kotlin.NoWhenBranchMatchedException, emitted by the compiler as the default branch.
  3. How do you evolve a sealed type in a published library without breaking consumers? → Treat a new subtype as a major version change, or design it open from the start with an Unknown/Other subtype and document that consumers must handle it. Some teams also offer a fold function with a default.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "sealed lets you skip else." The senior answer gives the 1.6/1.7 statement history, the leak points (else, expect, binary consumers, external data), NoWhenBranchMatchedException, and an evolution strategy for libraries.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout when had else -> showGenericError(). A new RequiresAuthentication result (3-D Secure) went to the generic error for two releases. About 4% of card payments in one region failed until someone read the code.

questions.subtopic: Sealed hierarchy package and module rules
questions.promptHtml: Where can subclasses of a sealed class or interface be declared? What about indirect subclasses, Java, and multiplatform?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Modularized Android apps hit these rules as soon as someone tries to spread a sealed hierarchy across feature modules.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Since Kotlin 1.5, direct subclasses must be in the same module and the same package as the sealed type, in any file. Before 1.5 they had to be in the same file. They can be top-level or nested in named classes or objects, but not local classes or anonymous objects. The restriction applies only to direct subtypes. If a direct subtype is open, anyone who can see it can extend it, and exhaustiveness then treats that whole branch as a single case. In multiplatform, direct subclasses must be in the same source set, and an expect sealed type needs else in common code.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• History:
Kotlin Where direct subclasses may live
1.0 nested inside the sealed class only
1.1 same file
1.5+ same module and same package (any file); sealed interfaces introduced
  • The package rule is literal. Module :core with package com.app.state and a subclass in :feature-x with the same package name is still rejected, because it's a different module. You can't split a sealed hierarchy across Gradle modules. That's deliberate: once a module is compiled, its hierarchy is closed.
  • Indirect subclasses:
    • sealed interface Error. Its direct subtypes must be in the same module and package.
    • sealed class IOError : Error. Its own subtypes are also restricted to its package and module.
    • open class CustomError : Error. This can be extended wherever it's visible, including other modules. To when (e: Error), the whole CustomError family is one branch (is CustomError).
    • This is the escape hatch for extensibility: sealed at the top for exhaustiveness, one open branch for plugins.
  • Constructors. Sealed class constructors are protected by default and may be private, never public or internal. Subclasses therefore must call through.
  • Java interop. The sealed constraint is enforced by the Kotlin compiler using Kotlin metadata. Don't count on the JVM or ART to stop Java code from implementing a Kotlin sealed interface. Whether a JVM PermittedSubclasses attribute is emitted depends on the Kotlin version and jvmTarget, so I wouldn't rely on it on Android. If Java code adds an implementation, Kotlin whens hit NoWhenBranchMatchedException at runtime.
  • Multiplatform:
    • Direct subclasses must be in the same source set as a non-expect sealed type.
    • With expect sealed class / actual, each side can add subclasses in its own source set, and intermediate source sets in a hierarchy can too.
    • That's why common-code when needs else.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// :core module, package com.app.error
sealed interface AppError
data class Network(val code: Int) : AppError          // OK: same module + package (any file)
sealed class Storage : AppError {
    data object DiskFull : Storage()
}
open class FeatureError(val message: String) : AppError   // deliberate open branch

// :feature-payments module
class CardRejected : FeatureError("rejected")          // OK: extends the open branch
// data class PaymentErr(val x: Int) : AppError        // ERROR: different module

fun handle(e: AppError) = when (e) {
    is Network -> "net ${e.code}"
