    is Storage -> "storage"                            // covers DiskFull and any future Storage subtype
    is FeatureError -> e.message                       // covers CardRejected and all others
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Trying to make a single app-wide sealed Event that every feature module extends. That's impossible by design. Push the sealed type into each feature, or use an open interface at the core.
  • Thinking that the same package name across modules is enough.
  • Declaring a subclass as a local class inside a function. That's not allowed, because subclasses need a proper qualified name.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a sealed class have subclasses in different files? → Yes, since 1.5, as long as they are in the same package and module.
  2. Can you have a sealed subclass of a sealed class? → Yes. It creates a nested closed sub-hierarchy that when can cover with one is or by enumerating its children.
  3. Why does KMP require else for expect sealed? → Each platform's actual can add subtypes common code can't see, so common code can't prove exhaustiveness.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "subclasses must be in the same file." That's outdated since 1.5. The senior answer gives the 1.5 rules, why cross-module is forbidden, the open-branch escape hatch and how it affects exhaustiveness, Java bypass risk, and KMP source-set rules.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: During modularization a team moved half of a sealed Destination into a feature module, hit compile errors, and "fixed" it by turning the hierarchy into an open interface with else branches everywhere. Exhaustive navigation checks were lost for good.

questions.promptHtml: What is a value class? How is it different from a typealias and from a data class wrapping one field?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Type-safe IDs and units are a common senior refactor. They want to see that you know the restrictions and that "zero cost" has conditions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A value class, @JvmInline value class UserId(val raw: String), wraps exactly one value and gives it a distinct compile-time type. At runtime the compiler usually passes the underlying String directly, with no wrapper object. A typealias is just another name for the same type, so a String still passes where a UserIdAlias is expected. A data class gives type safety but always allocates. A value class gives type safety plus, in most call sites, no allocation. The catch is that it gets boxed whenever it's used as another type: generic, nullable for primitives, or through an interface.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Syntax and versions. inline class was experimental, and the value class + @JvmInline form went stable in Kotlin 1.5. On the JVM, @JvmInline is required. The bare value keyword without it is reserved for a future multi-field value class model (Project Valhalla). Today a value class has exactly one primary-constructor property.
  • What's allowed: init blocks (good for validation), secondary constructors, functions, computed properties with no backing fields, implementing interfaces, and interface delegation (: Foo by wrapped).
  • What's not allowed:
    • extending classes (value classes are final and can't be in a class hierarchy)
    • extra stored properties, lateinit and delegated properties
    • ===, because identity is meaningless when there may be no object
  • Compilation sketch for fun load(id: UserId):
    • The function becomes load-<hash>(String id), a mangled name (see A1-Q064).
    • The class still exists with static helpers: constructor-impl (runs init validation and returns the raw value), box-impl, unbox-impl, equals-impl, hashCode-impl and toString-impl.
    • == between two value-class instances compares the underlying values.
  • Comparison:
typealias value class data class (1 field)
New type for the compiler no yes yes
String assignable to it yes no no
Runtime allocation none none unless boxed always
Validation on construction no init block init block
Java sees underlying type underlying type + mangled names normal class
copy/componentN n/a no yes
  • Good uses: IDs (UserId, OrderId), units (Millis, Px, Dp), validated strings (Email), and packing (Compose's Offset packs two floats into a Long, and Color wraps a ULong). The stdlib uses value classes for UInt, ULong, Duration and Result.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@JvmInline
value class UserId(val raw: String) {
    init { require(raw.isNotBlank()) { "blank id" } }
}

@JvmInline
value class Millis(val value: Long) {
    operator fun plus(o: Millis) = Millis(value + o.value)
}

typealias OrderIdAlias = String

fun fetchUser(id: UserId) { /* ... */ }
fun fetchOrder(id: OrderIdAlias) { /* ... */ }

fun demo(orderId: String, userId: String) {
    fetchOrder(userId)            // compiles: the typealias gives no protection
    // fetchUser(orderId)         // does not compile: a String is not a UserId
    fetchUser(UserId(userId))     // at runtime passes the String directly
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting typealiases to prevent ID mix-ups. They don't.
  • Assuming value classes are always free. Put them in List<UserId> and every element is a box (see A1-Q063).
  • Putting important invariants in init and then constructing the value from Java or reflection, which can bypass the Kotlin constructor path (see A1-Q064).
  • Writing @JvmInline without value, or value without @JvmInline on JVM targets. Both are compile errors.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a value class implement an interface? → Yes, but every use typed as that interface boxes.
  2. Can a value class wrap a nullable type or a generic type? → A nullable underlying type is allowed (value class Name(val s: String?)). Generic underlying types (value class Box<T>(val t: T)) are supported in recent Kotlin (I believe stable since 1.8; verify for your version) and are mapped to Any? or the upper bound at runtime.
  3. Why can't you use ===? → The value may exist only as a raw String or Long in one place and as a box in another, so identity would be unpredictable. The compiler forbids it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "a value class is an inline wrapper with no overhead." The senior answer covers the @JvmInline requirement and its Valhalla motivation, typealias vs value vs data class, init validation, the static -impl helpers, the stdlib and Compose examples, and that zero-cost is conditional.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team had fun transfer(fromAccount: String, toAccount: String) and a call site that swapped the arguments. Introducing AccountId value classes turned the bug class into a compile error at no measurable runtime cost on the hot path.

questions.promptHtml: When does a value class actually get boxed? What does that cost?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "Value classes are zero-cost" is the most common half-truth in Kotlin interviews. Knowing the boxing rules separates people who've profiled from people who've read the release notes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The rule of thumb is that a value class is boxed whenever it's used as some type other than itself. That means passing it as a generic T, storing it in a collection or Array<V>, using it through an interface it implements, treating it as Any, and making it nullable when the underlying type is a primitive (or is itself nullable). Used as its own non-null type in parameters, locals, fields and return values, it stays unboxed. Each box is a small heap allocation. One box is nothing, but millions per second in a scroll or render loop show up as GC churn and jank.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
For @JvmInline value class Px(val v: Float) : Comparable<Px>:

Usage Representation Why
fun f(p: Px) float used as itself
val p: Px local or field float used as itself
fun g(): Px float used as itself
fun <T> id(x: T) called with Px Px box generic erases to Object
List<Px>, Map<Px, X>, Set<Px> boxes collections hold objects
Array<Px> array of boxes (no PxArray exists; UIntArray is a stdlib special case)
val c: Comparable<Px> = p box used as interface
val n: Px? = p box float can't represent null
vararg p: Px array of boxes
lambda (Px) -> Unit box at the invoke boundary (the Function1.invoke(Object) signature) generic function type
  • Nullable with a non-null reference underlying type. For value class Name(val s: String), Name? can be represented as a nullable String without boxing, because null doesn't collide with any valid value. This is the documented design in the inline classes KEEP. Verify against bytecode for your version before relying on it in a hot path. For primitive-backed classes (Int, Long, Float), Px? must box.
  • Box, then unbox. fun <T> id(x: T): T = x; val p2: Px = id(p) boxes on the way in and unboxes on return. Generic utilities like maxOf, sortedBy { it.v } lambdas, Flow<Px>, StateFlow<Px> and LiveData<Px> all box.
  • Cost. A box of a float is an object header plus field. That's about 16 bytes on 64-bit ART (12-byte header, 4-byte float, padded to 8 bytes). At 60 fps, a list measuring 200 items × 10 Px boxes per frame = 2,000 allocations/frame ≈ 120k per second. Young-gen GC on ART handles that, but on low-end devices it adds measurable frame-time variance. Compose avoids this with sentinel values (Dp.Unspecified, Offset.Unspecified, implemented as NaN bit patterns) instead of nullable types.
  • The equals trap. Px boxes compare by value. (p as Any) == (p as Any) is true even when the two boxes are different objects. Identity checks are forbidden at compile time, but Java code or IdentityHashMap could still see distinct boxes.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@JvmInline value class Px(val v: Float)

fun widthOf(p: Px): Float = p.v                       // unboxed float param

fun sum(items: List<Px>): Px {                        // each element is a box
    var total = 0f
    for (p in items) total += p.v                     // unbox per element
    return Px(total)                                  // returned unboxed
}

fun sumFast(values: FloatArray): Px {                 // hot path: primitive storage
    var total = 0f
    for (v in values) total += v
    return Px(total)
}

// Nullable on a primitive-backed value class boxes; prefer a sentinel in hot code
val Unspecified = Px(Float.NaN)
fun Px.isSpecified() = !v.isNaN()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping IDs in value classes and then holding them in List<UserId>, Map<UserId, User> or StateFlow<UserId?>. You pay the box anyway. That's still usually fine for type safety, but don't claim a perf win.
  • Using Px? as "absent" in measure or layout code instead of a sentinel.
  • Assuming the JIT or AOT will remove boxes the way escape analysis sometimes does on the HotSpot JVM. Don't assume ART does it reliably.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you detect value-class boxing in a hot path? → Record allocations in the Android Studio Memory Profiler (or a Perfetto heap profile) during the interaction and look for allocations of the value-class type, or box-impl frames. Then read the bytecode via "Show Kotlin Bytecode" for the hot function.
  2. Is Result<T> boxed? → Result is a value class over Any?. It's generic, so it often ends up boxed when returned through generic APIs, lambdas or suspend boundaries. It's not free in hot loops either.
  3. Are there primitive collections to avoid boxing? → Yes. Use IntArray, LongArray and FloatArray, and androidx.collection's primitive collections (IntList, LongList, FloatList, IntIntMap, LongSparseArray). I believe the primitive list and map types arrived in androidx.collection 1.4.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "value classes are inlined, so no allocation." The senior answer gives the boxing table (generic, collection, interface, nullable primitive, lambda, vararg), the nullable-reference exception, approximate per-box cost, Compose's sentinel pattern, and how to measure with the Memory Profiler.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A canvas-based chart introduced Px? for optional axis bounds and drew 3,000 points per frame. Allocation tracking showed about 180k Px boxes per second while panning. Switching to a NaN sentinel took p95 frame time from about 22 ms to about 14 ms on a mid-tier device.

questions.subtopic: Value class name mangling and Java interop
questions.promptHtml: What is name mangling for value classes? What breaks when Java, reflection or serialization meets a value class?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: In mixed Kotlin/Java codebases and SDKs, value classes cause "method not found" confusion. Seniors know the escape hatches and their status.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A value class erases to its underlying type, so fun find(id: UserId) and fun find(raw: String) would both become find(String) on the JVM. To avoid that clash, Kotlin appends a hash to the name of functions that take value-class parameters, giving something like find-a1b2c3(String). Getters of value-class-typed properties are mangled too. Java can't call those names normally, and Java also can't call constructors that take value-class parameters. The fixes are @JvmName on functions, or @JvmExposeBoxed, which is experimental in Kotlin 2.2 and generates Java-callable boxed variants. Reflection-based libraries see only the underlying type, so I prefer codegen serializers like kotlinx.serialization, which support value classes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Why mangle. It prevents signature clashes like the one above. It also stops Java from calling a function with an unvalidated raw String, bypassing the type safety, by accident.
  • What gets mangled:
    • functions with value-class parameters
    • property accessors whose type is a value class (e.g., getId-<hash>() on a data class with val id: UserId)
    • members of the value class itself. Its methods become static -impl functions taking the underlying value.
    • Function return types alone historically didn't change the name in all cases. Check "Show Kotlin Bytecode" rather than guessing.
  • Constructors. A class Order(val id: OrderId) gets a JVM constructor with the underlying type plus a synthetic DefaultConstructorMarker parameter, so Java can't call it cleanly. A value class's own constructor isn't directly callable from Java either. Java would just pass the raw value around and never run init.
  • Escape hatches:
Tool Effect Status
@JvmName("findById") on a function stable, Java-callable name taking the underlying type stable; doesn't validate
@JvmExposeBoxed (class, constructor or function) generates a boxed, Java-callable variant, and Java can construct the value class (so init runs) experimental in Kotlin 2.2
-Xjvm-expose-boxed compiler flag as if the whole module were annotated with @JvmExposeBoxed experimental
plain wrapper data class for the Java API always works stable, allocates
  • Reflection and serialization:
    • Gson reflects on Java fields. The backing field of val id: UserId has type String, so Gson reads and writes raw strings and skips init validation. It can store garbage you assumed was impossible.
    • kotlinx.serialization supports @Serializable value classes and encodes them as the underlying value.
    • Moshi codegen works with Kotlin types. Value-class support depends on the version, so verify.
    • kotlin-reflect knows value classes. Plain Java reflection doesn't.
  • Mocking. Older MockK versions had trouble matching value-class arguments (any() vs unboxed parameters). Newer releases added support. Check your version's changelog.
  • Binary compatibility. The mangling hash is derived from the signature. Renaming a value class or changing its underlying type changes the mangled names, so it's a binary-incompatible change for prebuilt consumers, even when the source still compiles.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@JvmInline value class UserId(val raw: String)

class UserApi {
    fun find(id: UserId): User = TODO()                 // JVM: find-<hash>(String), invisible to Java

    @JvmName("findById")
    fun findForJava(id: UserId): User = find(id)        // JVM: findById(String), Java-callable
}

// Kotlin 2.2, experimental: also expose boxed forms to Java
// (add whatever opt-in the 2.2 docs require for this experimental annotation)
@JvmExposeBoxed
@JvmInline value class OrderId(val raw: String) {
    init { require(raw.startsWith("ord_")) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Introducing value classes in a public SDK used from Java without a plan for Java callers. They'll see mangled names or nothing.
  • Trusting init validation when the data comes in through Gson or Java reflection.
  • Thinking @JvmName keeps type safety for Java callers. Java passes a raw String with no validation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does Kotlin mangle instead of just overloading on the wrapper type? → Because the JVM signature uses the erased underlying type, so true overloading by wrapper is impossible without boxing.
  2. Can you put @JvmName on a member of an interface or an open function? → Restrictions apply: @JvmName isn't allowed on open or override members, because renaming would break virtual dispatch. Use a final wrapper function instead.
  3. How do you safely evolve a value class in a published library? → Treat its name and underlying type as ABI. Track the API with an ABI validator (the binary-compatibility-validator plugin, or the experimental ABI validation in the Kotlin Gradle plugin in 2.2), and expose stable @JvmName entry points for Java.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "Java can't easily call it." The senior answer explains why mangling exists, what's mangled (params, accessors, -impl members), DefaultConstructorMarker constructors, @JvmName vs experimental @JvmExposeBoxed, Gson bypassing init, and ABI implications.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Kotlin SDK switched String IDs to value classes in a minor release. Java-based host apps got NoSuchMethodError: getId() at runtime, because the getter became getId-<hash>(). The release had to be reverted and reissued as a major version.

questions.promptHtml: How do Kotlin interfaces with method bodies compile to JVM bytecode, and what changed with Kotlin 2.2? When would you use an abstract class instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's a Java interop and binary-compatibility issue that SDK and platform teams hit. The abstract-class question checks that you can model state correctly.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Before Kotlin 2.2, a method body in a Kotlin interface wasn't a Java 8 default method by default. Kotlin put the body in a static nested DefaultImpls class, and every Kotlin implementing class got a bridge method calling it. Java implementors had to implement every method themselves. You could opt into real JVM default methods with -Xjvm-default=all or all-compatibility. Since Kotlin 2.2 there's a stable -jvm-default option whose default is enable: real default methods plus DefaultImpls and bridges kept for compatibility. no-compatibility drops the compatibility layer, and disable is the old behavior. I use an abstract class when I need constructor state or protected members. Otherwise I use an interface, because a class can implement many of them.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Interfaces in Kotlin can declare abstract members, members with bodies, and properties. Properties are either abstract or have getters only: no backing fields, so no state. Members are open. They can't have protected or internal-constructor state.
  • Conflict resolution. If a class inherits the same member from two interfaces, it must override it and can call each one with super<A>.foo() and super<B>.foo().
  • Compilation modes:
Mode Interface method bodies DefaultImpls class Bridges in Kotlin implementors Java implementor must implement?
pre-2.2 default / disable none in interface yes yes yes, all methods
-Xjvm-default=all-compatibility (pre-2.2) / enable (2.2 default) JVM default methods yes, kept for old callers yes no
-Xjvm-default=all (pre-2.2) / no-compatibility JVM default methods no no no
  • Kotlin 2.2 changes. -jvm-default is stable and replaces the deprecated -Xjvm-default. In Gradle: kotlin { compilerOptions { jvmDefault = JvmDefaultMode.NO_COMPATIBILITY } }. The old @JvmDefault annotation is long deprecated and removed. Don't use it.
  • Why compatibility matters. Binaries compiled in the old mode call Iface$DefaultImpls.method(this). If a library drops DefaultImpls (no-compatibility) and a consumer's prebuilt binary still references it, you get NoClassDefFoundError or NoSuchMethodError at runtime (see A1-Q075).
  • Android. Default interface methods require Java 8 language features. D8 desugars them for any minSdk (via companion classes), so you can use them freely in app code. The binary-compatibility concerns are about libraries.
  • Abstract class vs interface:
Need Choose
constructor parameters / stored state abstract class
protected helpers for subclasses abstract class
a type that mixes into many classes interface
a fake or test double without inheritance constraints interface
a template method with a fixed algorithm abstract class with final orchestration and abstract steps

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface Clickable {
    fun click()
    fun describe(): String = "clickable"          // body → default method (2.2 default) or DefaultImpls (disable)
}
interface Focusable {
    val focusOrder: Int get() = 0                 // property with getter, no backing field
    fun describe(): String = "focusable"
}

class Button : Clickable, Focusable {
    override fun click() {}
    override fun describe() = super<Clickable>.describe() + "+" + super<Focusable>.describe()   // must resolve conflict
}

abstract class BaseScreen(protected val analytics: Analytics) {   // state + protected → abstract class
    fun onShown() { analytics.track(screenName()) }               // final template method
    protected abstract fun screenName(): String
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming Java implementors of a Kotlin interface get its default bodies. That's only true when compiled in enable or no-compatibility mode (or -Xjvm-default=all* before 2.2).
  • Flipping a library to no-compatibility in a minor release.
  • Putting val cache = mutableMapOf<…>() in an interface. That's not allowed. A getter that returns a new map on every call compiles, but it's a bug.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does the body live in disable mode? → In a generated static nested class Iface$DefaultImpls, as a static method taking the receiver as its first parameter. Kotlin implementors get bridge methods that call it.
  2. Can an interface have a private function? → Yes, a private member with a body works as a helper. It compiles to a private method (or into DefaultImpls, depending on the mode).
  3. If I add a new method with a body to a published Kotlin interface, is that binary-compatible for Java implementors? → In enable or no-compatibility mode, yes: they inherit the JVM default. In disable mode, no: existing Java implementors lack the method, and calls fail with AbstractMethodError.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "interfaces can have default implementations, unlike Java 7." The senior answer explains DefaultImpls and bridges, the -Xjvm-default modes, the Kotlin 2.2 -jvm-default default of enable and what no-compatibility removes, the binary-compatibility consequences, super<A> conflict resolution, and the abstract-class criteria.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An SDK added fun onRetry() {} with an empty body to a listener interface, compiled in the old mode. Java host apps implementing the listener crashed with AbstractMethodError when the SDK called onRetry().

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the exact order in which Kotlin runs constructors, property initializers and init blocks, including with inheritance and secondary constructors.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "Predict the output" questions are common, and init-order bugs produce nulls in non-null types. You need the exact model.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For class D(...) : B(args), the arguments to B are evaluated first. Then B fully initializes: its property initializers and init blocks run top to bottom in source order. Then D's property initializers and init blocks run top to bottom in source order, interleaved exactly as written. Only after that does the body of whatever secondary constructor was called run. Every secondary constructor must delegate to the primary, directly or through another secondary, so the primary path and all initializers run before any secondary body.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Bytecode view. There's only one real initialization path. The primary constructor's JVM <init> contains, in order:
    1. super(...) with the evaluated arguments
    2. each property initializer and init block, in textual order
    3. nothing else
  • A secondary constructor's <init> calls this(...) (the primary) first, then runs its own body.
new D("a")  [secondary ctor]
  └─ this("a", 0)            [primary]
       ├─ evaluate B's ctor args
       ├─ B.<init>
       │    ├─ B property initializers + init blocks (textual order)
       ├─ D property initializers + init blocks (textual order)
  └─ secondary body
  • Textual order is what matters. An init block placed above a property declaration runs before that property is assigned. If the code reads the property directly, the compiler stops you ("Variable must be initialized"). If it reads it through a function or getter, the compiler can't see it, and you read the default JVM value: null, 0 or false, even for non-null types. See A1-Q070.
  • Classes with no primary constructor. Each secondary constructor calls super(...) directly, and the initializers and init blocks still run (they're inlined into each such constructor) before the secondary body.
  • Overridden properties. If B declares open val size = 1 and D overrides it with override val size = 2, there are two backing fields. During B's init, any virtual call to size dispatches to D's getter, which returns D's still-unassigned field: 0. This is the "open member in constructor" bug (A1-Q071).
  • Companion objects are initialized when the class is first loaded, before any instance initialization (K2a has the details).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
open class Base(val name: String) {
    init { println("2. Base init, name=$name") }
    open val tag: String = "base".also { println("3. Base tag initializer") }
}

class Child(name: String, val level: Int) : Base(name.also { println("1. Base arg evaluated") }) {
    init { println("4. Child init #1, level=$level") }
    override val tag: String = "child".also { println("5. Child tag initializer") }
    init { println("6. Child init #2") }

    constructor(name: String) : this(name, 0) { println("7. Secondary body") }
}

fun main() { Child("x") }
// Prints 1 → 7 in order.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking init blocks run before property initializers, or that all init blocks run together. Both are wrong. It's purely textual order.
  • Thinking secondary constructor bodies run before initializers.
  • Reading a later-declared property via a helper function in init and getting null.
  • Expecting the Base part to see the Child values of overridden properties during construction.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can primary constructor parameters be used in initializers? → Yes. They're in scope in property initializers and init blocks (but not in member functions, unless declared val/var).
  2. What's the order between companion object init and instance init? → The companion (static) initializer runs once at class initialization, before the first instance is constructed.
  3. How does lateinit interact with init order? → It has no initializer, so nothing runs for it. Reading it before assignment throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException, which at least fails loudly, unlike a silent null.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "init blocks run when the object is created." The senior answer explains superclass first, base-arg evaluation, textual interleaving of initializers and init, secondary bodies last, the single JVM <init> model, and the default-value hole for indirect reads and overridden properties.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A refactor moved an init { loadFromDisk() } block to the top of a class "for readability". A property declared below it, with an initializer, then overwrote the loaded value on every construction, silently resetting the user's settings (see A1-Q070).

questions.promptHtml: What exactly is an object expression? What does it capture, and what's its type when you return it from a function?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Object expressions are everywhere in Android callbacks. The typing rule and the capture behavior are subtle, and both cause bugs or confusing compile errors.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: object : Foo(), Bar { ... } creates a new instance of an unnamed class each time the expression runs. It can extend at most one class and any number of interfaces. Unlike Java, it can capture and mutate local vars (Kotlin wraps them in Ref holders), and it captures the outer this if it uses outer members. The anonymous type is visible only from local or private, non-inline declarations. If you return it from a public function, the type becomes the declared supertype, or Any if there's none, and the extra members disappear.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Compilation. It becomes a synthetic class like MainActivity$onCreate$1 with fields for captured values. Using an outer member adds a reference to the outer instance. A captured var becomes a shared Ref.IntRef or Ref.ObjectRef so both sides see writes. The details of Ref boxing belong to K3a.
  • New instance per evaluation. An object expression inside onBindViewHolder allocates every bind. Hoist it if it's stateless.
  • Typing rules (from the language docs):
    • Local, or private and non-inline: the actual anonymous type is kept, so its members are accessible.
    • Public, protected, internal, or private inline: the type is the declared supertype, or Any if none, so extra members are invisible.
  • Object expression vs object declaration vs companion:
    • An expression is evaluated immediately where it's used, and each time.
    • An object declaration is a lazily initialized singleton.
    • A companion is tied to class loading. Declarations and companions are covered in K2a.
  • Object expression vs lambda for interfaces. For a single-method interface, a lambda (SAM conversion) is shorter. The SAM details are in K3b. Use an object expression when you need several methods, state fields, an init, or this to refer to the listener itself, for example to unregister from inside the callback.
  • Ad-hoc structs. val point = object { val x = 1; val y = 2 } works locally. It's fine for a quick local grouping and pointless in APIs.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Screen {
    private fun makeCounter() = object {          // private → anonymous type kept
        var clicks = 0
        fun inc() { clicks++ }
    }

    fun publicCounter() = object {                // public → type is Any
        var clicks = 0
    }

    fun demo(sensorManager: SensorManager, sensor: Sensor) {
        makeCounter().inc()                       // OK
        // publicCounter().clicks                 // compile error: Any has no 'clicks'

        var events = 0                            // captured var → Ref.IntRef
        val listener = object : SensorEventListener {
            override fun onSensorChanged(e: SensorEvent) {
                if (++events >= 10) sensorManager.unregisterListener(this)   // 'this' = the listener
            }
            override fun onAccuracyChanged(s: Sensor, accuracy: Int) {}
        }
        sensorManager.registerListener(listener, sensor, SensorManager.SENSOR_DELAY_UI)
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using this inside an object expression and expecting the Activity. It's the anonymous object. Use this@MainActivity.
  • Creating object-expression listeners in hot paths (bind, draw, compose without remember).
  • Returning an anonymous object from a public function and wondering why members are unresolved.
  • Capturing an Activity in a listener registered with a singleton, which is the same leak as an inner class (see A1-Q069).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can an object expression have a constructor? → No constructor, but it can pass arguments to its superclass constructor (object : Base(42) {}) and have init blocks.
  2. Why can Kotlin mutate captured locals when Java can't? → Kotlin wraps captured vars in a heap Ref object, while Java requires effectively final locals. The cost is an allocation and no thread safety.
  3. Does an object expression always capture the outer class? → No. In current Kotlin it captures the outer this only if the body references outer members or this@Outer. Verify in bytecode if it matters for a leak.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "it's an anonymous class like Java's." The senior answer covers the new instance per evaluation, Ref capture of vars, conditional outer capture, the local/private vs public typing rule, the this ambiguity, and when to pick an object expression over a SAM lambda.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An object : ViewTreeObserver.OnGlobalLayoutListener was added in onBindViewHolder and never removed. Each bind added another listener, and after scrolling 500 rows layout passes took over 30 ms.

questions.promptHtml: How is internal implemented on the JVM? What are its practical limits in a multi-module Android app or a published library?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Platform and modularization work leans on internal for encapsulation. Seniors know it's a compiler-level fence, not a runtime one, and how it interacts with tests, Java and R8.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: internal exists only in Kotlin's type system. In bytecode, internal classes and members are public. To discourage Java callers, internal member names are mangled with the module name, like refresh$feature_feed_release, but internal classes keep their names. A module is one compilation unit: a Gradle source set, with test and androidTest compilations treated as friends that can see main's internals. So Java and reflection can still reach internal code, and R8 may rename it anyway. I use internal plus Gradle module boundaries as an architecture fence, and explicitApi() and an ABI check for libraries.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Bytecode.
    • internal class Foo → public final class Foo.
    • internal fun bar() in a class → public final bar$moduleName().
    • The Kotlin metadata records the true visibility, so other Kotlin modules get a compile error and Kotlin consumers are properly blocked.
  • Module name. It comes from the Gradle module and the build variant (for Android, often <module>_<variant>). That's why mangled names change between debug and release, or if you rename the module. Never hard-code them.
  • Friend modules. Test source sets are associated compilations, so unit tests can call internal code without @VisibleForTesting gymnastics. Other modules can't, unless they're configured as friends (-Xfriend-paths, an unsupported internal flag). Don't build an architecture on that.
  • Java callers. Java in another module can call public internal classes, and mangled members if it spells the name. Lint and code review are the only fence there.
  • Inline functions. A public inline fun can't reference internal declarations, because the body is copied into the caller's module. Mark those helpers @PublishedApi internal, which makes them effectively public ABI (details in K3a).
  • R8. In an app, R8 renames everything not kept anyway, so mangling doesn't matter after shrinking. In a library AAR, consumer keep rules and reflection decide what survives.
  • Library hygiene:
    • explicitApi() forces explicit modifiers.
    • An ABI dump (the binary-compatibility-validator Gradle plugin, or the experimental ABI validation in the Kotlin Gradle plugin since 2.2) catches accidental public surface and internal changes that leak via @PublishedApi.
:core:network  (internal class HttpClientFactory)    →  bytecode: public class HttpClientFactory
      ▲                                                      Kotlin in :feature:feed: compile error
      │ implementation(project(":core:network"))              Java in :feature:feed: compiles (!)
:feature:feed

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// :core:network
internal class TokenCache {                  // JVM: public final class TokenCache
    internal fun clear() {}                  // JVM: public final void clear$network_release()
}

public class NetworkApi internal constructor(private val cache: TokenCache)   // public type, module-only creation

@PublishedApi internal fun logCall(name: String) = println(name)
public inline fun <T> traced(name: String, block: () -> T): T {
    logCall(name)                            // allowed only because of @PublishedApi
    return block()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling internal "module-private" in a security discussion. It isn't a runtime boundary.
  • Using @PublishedApi casually. It turns internal helpers into permanent ABI.
  • Expecting internal to hide things inside a single huge :app module. If everything is in one module, everything is visible. internal only gets its power from modularization.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why mangle members but not classes? → Members can clash, and mangling discourages Java calls. Class names are referenced by FQN and are needed for Java interop and reflection. Kotlin relies on metadata for classes.
  2. Can a test in :app access internal in :core? → No. Only :core's own test source sets are friends.
  3. You need a :feature module to call a :core API that only it should use. What do you do? → Make it public with an opt-in requirement annotation (@RequiresOptIn with level ERROR), or move the API into a small shared module. Don't abuse friend paths.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "internal means visible in the same module." The senior answer explains public-in-bytecode, member-name mangling with module and variant, test friend compilations, Java and reflection bypass, @PublishedApi ABI, R8 effects, and explicitApi() plus ABI validation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team's "internal" analytics initializer was called via its mangled name from a Java module after a hasty merge. Renaming the Gradle module during a restructure caused NoSuchMethodError crashes on launch for that variant only.

questions.contextHtml:
A photo app (1.2M DAU) shows an upload-progress banner on GalleryActivity. Since release 7.4, Crashlytics shows an OutOfMemoryError cluster (0.3% of sessions, mostly 3 GB RAM devices) after users rotate or reopen the gallery a few times. A teammate blames Glide's bitmap cache, and that's a red herring: the cache size didn't change. LeakCanary in the internal build reports:

┬─── UploadManager (singleton)
│    ↓ UploadManager.listeners (ArrayList, size=7)
├─── GalleryActivity$ProgressListener
│    ↓ GalleryActivity$ProgressListener.this$0
╰→── GalleryActivity  (mDestroyed = true)   Retaining 38.2 MB in 412,551 objects
class GalleryActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private lateinit var binding: ActivityGalleryBinding

    inner class ProgressListener : UploadManager.Listener {
        override fun onProgress(id: String, percent: Int) {
            binding.uploadBanner.progress = percent
        }
    }

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        binding = ActivityGalleryBinding.inflate(layoutInflater)
        setContentView(binding.root)
        UploadManager.addListener(ProgressListener())
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain the mechanism, and fix it properly.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make the listener a WeakReference" or "Glide is leaking, call Glide.get(this).clearMemory()". The first patches the symptom and can drop progress updates while the screen is visible, if the weak reference is collected. The second ignores the trace. Neither explains why inner matters or why there are 7 listeners.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Does UploadManager ever remove listeners? That decides whether this is a leak or just late cleanup.
    • Do uploads need to update the UI while the Activity is in the background? That decides between STARTED and CREATED scope.
    • Is UploadManager process-wide or Hilt @Singleton? It's the same lifetime either way.
  2. Immediate mitigation: ship a hotfix that removes the listener in onDestroy. It's a tiny, low-risk diff.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. An inner-class listener held by a singleton and never removed. The trace shows this$0 and listener count 7, one per Activity instance.
    2. Glide cache growth. Unlikely: the trace's retaining path doesn't go through Glide.
    3. View binding retained separately. It's part of the same retained Activity.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • LeakCanary trace (done).
    • Android Studio Memory Profiler: rotate 5 times, force GC, dump the heap, and count GalleryActivity instances (expect 6 retained).
    • After the fix, repeat and expect 1.
    • Add a Log.d of listeners.size in debug builds.
  5. Root cause: inner class ProgressListener compiles with a synthetic this$0 field pointing at the GalleryActivity that created it. UploadManager lives for the whole process and keeps every listener in an ArrayList. Each rotation creates a new Activity and a new listener, and the old one is never removed. Each destroyed Activity (about 5 MB with its view tree) stays strongly reachable. That's 7 instances × about 5 MB ≈ 38 MB, matching LeakCanary. inner is needed here only because the body uses binding. The bug is the lifetime mismatch, not the keyword itself.
  6. Fix:
    • Short term: keep one listener instance and pair add and remove with the lifecycle.
    • Long term: invert the dependency. UploadManager exposes a StateFlow of progress, and the UI collects it lifecycle-aware, so the UI never registers a callback with a singleton (collection details in F5).
class GalleryActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private lateinit var binding: ActivityGalleryBinding
    private val listener = UploadManager.Listener { _, percent ->   // assumes Listener is a fun interface; otherwise an object expression
        binding.uploadBanner.progress = percent
    }

    override fun onStart() { super.onStart(); UploadManager.addListener(listener) }
    override fun onStop() { UploadManager.removeListener(listener); super.onStop() }
}

// Long term: no callbacks into the UI from the singleton
object UploadManager {
    private val _progress = MutableStateFlow<Map<String, Int>>(emptyMap())
    val progress: StateFlow<Map<String, Int>> = _progress.asStateFlow()
}
// UI: lifecycleScope.launch { repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) { manager.progress.collect { … } } }
  1. Prevention:
    • Run LeakCanary in QA builds, and add a leak assertion in instrumented tests (DetectLeaksAfterTestSuccess from leakcanary-android-instrumentation).
    • Review checklist: "any add*Listener on a long-lived object has a matching remove in the mirror lifecycle callback."
    • Prefer Flow exposure from singletons over listener lists.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • I wouldn't make UploadManager hold WeakReferences as the primary fix. It hides ownership bugs, and listeners passed as lambdas can be collected while the screen is still visible, so progress stops updating.
    • I wouldn't just change inner to nested and pass the Activity in. That keeps the same leak with extra steps.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the listener were a lambda instead of an inner class? → Same leak. A lambda touching binding captures the Activity.
  • Why does it show mostly on 3 GB devices? → The heap limit is lower there (largeHeap not set), so 38 MB of retained Activities plus bitmaps crosses it sooner. Flagship devices just GC more.
  • Would onDestroy removal be enough? → It fixes the leak, but the Activity would still receive updates while stopped. onStart/onStop matches the visible lifetime.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: In a media app, a singleton player kept inner-class callbacks from every screen that ever showed a mini-player. Heap dumps showed 20+ destroyed Activities after an hour of use. Converting the player to expose a StateFlow removed the whole category of leak, and the OOM cluster went to zero in the next release.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames Glide or GC. Can't explain this$0.
  • Hire: identifies inner class + singleton + no unregister, and fixes with paired lifecycle add and remove.
  • Strong hire: explains the reachability math from the trace, chooses a lifecycle-matched scope, rejects WeakReference as the main fix with reasons, and proposes Flow exposure plus leak checks in CI.

questions.contextHtml:
A fintech-style budgeting app (600k DAU) shipped 9.1. Within 24h, support tickets jumped: "I get logged out every time I reopen the app". About 100% of cold starts show the login screen. Warm resumes are fine. Debug builds use FakeSessionManager, so QA missed it. One engineer suspects the EncryptedSharedPreferences keyset got corrupted after an AndroidX Security bump in the same release. That's a red herring: the key is readable in a debugger. The only change to this class in 9.1 was a "cleanup" PR that moved the init block to the top:

class SessionManager(context: Context) {

    init {
        restore()
    }

    private val prefs: SharedPreferences =
        context.getSharedPreferences("session", Context.MODE_PRIVATE)

    var token: String? = null
        private set

    val isLoggedIn: Boolean get() = token != null

    private fun restore() {
        token = prefs.getString("token", null)
    }
}

Strangely, Crashlytics shows no new crash from SessionManager, and the team expected one if prefs were null.
questions.promptHtml: What exactly is wrong? Why is there no crash? Fix it and prevent the class of bug.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The prefs are being cleared. Check EncryptedSharedPreferences." Or "move init to the bottom" with no explanation. That answer can't explain the missing crash, and it's fragile: the next reorder breaks it again.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Is the snippet exactly what shipped, or is prefs actually declared above init in the release branch? The order is everything here.
    • Is SessionManager constructed once via Hilt @Singleton?
    • Did any other code write token during startup?
  2. Immediate mitigation: revert the reorder PR in a hotfix. It's tiny and safe. Tokens were never deleted from disk, so users are restored without re-login once the fix ships.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. An init-order bug in this class (the only diff).
    2. A corrupted encrypted prefs keyset (contradicted: the value reads fine in a debugger).
    3. A server-side token invalidation (contradicted: warm resumes keep working).
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • A unit test with Robolectric or a fake Context that writes a token, constructs SessionManager and asserts isLoggedIn.
    • A breakpoint in restore() and on the token field's write (field watchpoint) to see the second write.
    • "Show Kotlin Bytecode" on the class to see the order inside <init>.
  5. Root cause: initializers and init blocks run in textual order inside one JVM <init>, so the sequence is init { restore() } → prefs = … → token = null. In the snippet as written, restore() runs while prefs is still null. The compiler doesn't catch it, because the read happens inside a function. That would throw an NPE. The release branch had kept prefs above init, and only the init block moved above token, so restore() succeeded and set token. Then the token's own initializer = null ran and overwrote it. That explains no crash, logged out on every cold start, and the debugger showing a valid stored value. Both orderings are broken. One crashes, one fails silently.
<init>:  super()  →  init{ restore() }  →  prefs = ...  →  token = null   ← overwrites restored value
  1. Fix:
    • Short term: put init after all properties it touches.
    • Better: remove the ordering dependency entirely. Compute state in the initializer itself, or make reads go through the source of truth.
class SessionManager(context: Context) {
    private val prefs: SharedPreferences =
        context.getSharedPreferences("session", Context.MODE_PRIVATE)

    var token: String? = prefs.getString("token", null)   // initialized from source; no init block needed
        private set

    val isLoggedIn: Boolean get() = token != null

    fun save(newToken: String) {
        prefs.edit().putString("token", newToken).apply()
        token = newToken
    }
}
  • Long term: move session storage to DataStore exposed as Flow<Session?> (that's a separate design discussion), and keep disk I/O out of constructors. getSharedPreferences reads the file on a background thread, but the first getString blocks until the load finishes. That's a startup StrictMode or ANR risk on the main thread.
  1. Prevention:
    • A regression unit test: "restores token from storage".
    • Review rule: init blocks must not call member functions that read properties, and init goes after property declarations.
    • Turn on the IDE/detekt inspections around calling non-final or member functions from constructors and property-declaration ordering. Check your detekt version's rule set for the exact names.
    • Release checklist: test cold start in a release-like build, not only with fakes.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • I wouldn't "fix" it with lateinit var token. It's nullable, which lateinit doesn't allow anyway, and it hides the real ordering problem.
    • I wouldn't add by lazy around prefs as a band-aid without fixing the token = null overwrite. The silent reset would remain.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why didn't the compiler warn? → Definite-assignment analysis only checks direct reads in initializers and init. Calls through functions are opaque to it.
  • Would making restore() private inline help? → Since an inline body is copied in, the compiler might then see the direct read and error. That's a fragile accident, not a design.
  • What if token had no initializer? → A var with no initializer must be assigned in init (definitely assigned) or be lateinit/abstract. Assigning only inside restore() doesn't count, so it wouldn't compile. That's a nice illustration of why direct assignment in init is safer than helper calls.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "sort members alphabetically" IDE action applied across a module reordered property declarations in three classes. One of them was a feature-flag cache whose defaults overwrote remote values on every cold start. The fix was trivial. The lesson was to ban order-dependent init patterns and add one test per stateful constructor.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: chases EncryptedSharedPreferences. Can't explain the textual order.
  • Hire: identifies the reorder, explains the token = null overwrite, fixes the order.
  • Strong hire: explains both failure modes (NPE vs silent overwrite) and why no crash, why the compiler can't see it, removes the ordering dependency structurally, and adds a test plus a review rule.

questions.contextHtml:
Release 5.12 of a delivery app (2.5M DAU, minSdk 24) added PhoneInputView, a custom field used on checkout and profile screens. Crash-free sessions dropped from 99.82% to 99.41% within 6 hours of a 20% staged rollout. The top crash appears only on the profile screen, and only when the XML layout sets a default android:text. Checkout uses the same view without android:text and is clean. Someone points at a Samsung-only OEM keyboard bug, because 60% of crashes are Samsung. That's a red herring: Samsung is 58% of the user base.

Fatal Exception: java.lang.NullPointerException
  Attempt to invoke virtual method 'java.lang.String com.app.PhoneFormatter.format(java.lang.CharSequence)' on a null object reference
    at com.app.ui.PhoneInputView.setText(PhoneInputView.kt:21)
    at android.widget.TextView.setText(TextView.java)
    at android.widget.TextView.<init>(TextView.java)
    at android.widget.EditText.<init>(EditText.java)
    at androidx.appcompat.widget.AppCompatEditText.<init>(AppCompatEditText.java)
    at com.app.ui.PhoneInputView.<init>(PhoneInputView.kt:12)
class PhoneInputView @JvmOverloads constructor(
    context: Context, attrs: AttributeSet? = null
) : AppCompatEditText(context, attrs) {

    private val formatter = PhoneFormatter(Locale.getDefault())

    override fun setText(text: CharSequence?, type: BufferType?) {
        super.setText(formatter.format(text ?: ""), type)
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through how you'd handle this incident, the root cause, and the right fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make formatter lazy" or "add ?., since Kotlin says it's non-null." by lazy doesn't help: the delegate field itself is still null when the superclass constructor calls setText, so you get the same NPE one frame deeper. Adding ?. on a non-null type gets a compiler warning, and the answer doesn't explain how a non-null val can be null at all.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • What percentage of the rollout cohort hits the profile screen? That sizes the impact.
    • Is the crash also triggered by state restoration? TextView restores text in onRestoreInstanceState, so a rotation on checkout might hit a related path later.
    • Do any other custom views in the module override methods the framework calls from its constructor?
  2. Immediate mitigation: halt the staged rollout at 20% in Play Console. If a server-driven layout flag exists, swap the profile screen to the old field. Otherwise ship a hotfix (step 6, short term).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. A superclass constructor calling an overridden method before subclass fields are initialized. The stack shows TextView.<init> → setText → our override, and it only fails when android:text is set.
    2. A Samsung keyboard issue. Rejected: the device share mirrors the user base, and the stack is in the constructor, not input handling.
    3. Locale-dependent PhoneFormatter init failing. Rejected: the formatter is null, not throwing.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Reproduce with an instrumented test or a Compose/View preview that inflates the layout with android:text.
    • Confirm with a breakpoint in setText that this.formatter == null while PhoneInputView.<init> is still on the stack.
    • Check Crashlytics custom keys for screen name to confirm 100% profile.
  5. Root cause: Kotlin init order is superclass first. AppCompatEditText(context, attrs) → TextView.<init> reads the android:text attribute and calls the virtual setText(CharSequence, BufferType). Dispatch goes to our override, but PhoneInputView's property initializers haven't run yet, because they execute after super(...) returns. So the formatter backing field holds the JVM default, null, even though Kotlin types it as non-null. Kotlin doesn't insert null checks when reading its own non-null private fields, so we get a raw JVM NPE. Checkout is clean because without android:text the constructor never calls setText.
PhoneInputView.<init>
  └─ super(context, attrs)  ── TextView.<init> ── setText(xmlText) ──► PhoneInputView.setText  (formatter == null) 💥
  └─ formatter = PhoneFormatter(...)   ← never reached
  1. Fix:
    • Short term (hotfix): tolerate the pre-init call explicitly and format later.
    • Long term: don't override framework methods that the superclass constructor calls. Formatting belongs in a TextWatcher or InputFilter installed in init, or in the ViewModel. Stop intercepting setText.
class PhoneInputView @JvmOverloads constructor(
    context: Context, attrs: AttributeSet? = null
) : AppCompatEditText(context, attrs) {

    private val formatter = PhoneFormatter(Locale.getDefault())
    private var selfUpdate = false

    init {
        // Runs after super() and after formatter is assigned; reformat whatever XML set
        setText(text)
        addTextChangedListener(object : TextWatcher {
            override fun beforeTextChanged(s: CharSequence?, st: Int, c: Int, a: Int) {}
            override fun onTextChanged(s: CharSequence?, st: Int, b: Int, c: Int) {}
            override fun afterTextChanged(s: Editable) {
                if (selfUpdate) return
                selfUpdate = true
                val formatted = formatter.format(s)
                if (formatted != s.toString()) s.replace(0, s.length, formatted)
                selfUpdate = false
            }
        })
    }
}

For the hotfix-only path, the minimal change is to keep the override and guard it: @Suppress("SENSELESS_COMPARISON") if (formatter == null) return super.setText(text, type). Comment it as a construction-time guard. It's ugly but safe, and the next release replaces it with the version above. 7. Prevention:

  • Lint and review rule: no overriding of setText, setBackground*, setLayoutParams, onMeasure and similar in custom Views unless the override is safe to call before subclass init.
  • Keep the IDE inspection "Calling non-final function in constructor" / "Accessing non-final property in constructor" enabled for our own base classes.
  • Screenshot or instrumented tests that inflate every custom view with every XML attribute set.
  • Staged rollout with a crash-free-sessions gate (auto-halt below 99.7%).
  1. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • I wouldn't use by lazy, which has the same NPE on the delegate field. I wouldn't use lateinit either, which throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException instead.
    • I wouldn't move formatting into the companion object as a static formatter. It fixes the null, but it makes locale changes stale for the whole process.
    • I wouldn't wrap the whole override in try/catch. That would hide real formatting bugs.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does the same problem exist in our own Kotlin base classes? → Yes. abstract class BaseViewModel { init { setup() } } with abstract fun setup() lets subclasses touch unassigned fields. Pass dependencies in as constructor parameters, or call setup explicitly after construction.
  • Why doesn't Kotlin protect non-null vals here? → Null safety relies on initialization happening before use, and the JVM permits virtual calls from constructors. The compiler only warns (the inspection) for calls from the class's own constructor, and can't see framework-side calls.
  • Could Compose avoid this? → In Compose there are no View constructors to override. Formatting is a VisualTransformation or input transformation applied to state, which removes this whole category of bug.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A custom RecyclerView subclass overrode setLayoutManager to attach a scroll helper stored in a field. Inflation from XML with app:layoutManager crashed on one screen only. Removing the override and wiring the helper in init was a five-line fix after two days of blaming a library upgrade.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests lazy/?., can't explain a null non-null property, chases Samsung.
  • Hire: reads the stack, explains superclass-first init and virtual dispatch, fixes by moving formatting out of the override.
  • Strong hire: also explains why lazy/lateinit fail, why checkout is clean, generalizes to base classes, and adds rollout gates and inflation tests.

questions.contextHtml: A super-app has 34 Gradle feature modules and 45 Android engineers. Analytics is modeled as one sealed interface AnalyticsEvent in :core:analytics, with 310 subtypes (data classes) in a 2,800-line file, so the tracker's when is exhaustive. Every feature that adds an event edits :core:analytics. Since that module is depended on by everything, each event change invalidates about 30 modules. Incremental CI builds went from about 6 min to about 19 min p50. The core file is the top source of merge conflicts (about 25 per week). A tech lead proposes "move each feature's events into its feature module but keep them in the sealed interface", which won't compile. Product insists that "no event may be silently dropped by the tracker".
questions.promptHtml: How would you restructure this? What do you give up?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Just make it an open interface and add else -> in the tracker." That fixes the build but drops the one guarantee product asked for, silently. Or "split the file into several files in the same module", which helps merge conflicts but not the rebuild fan-out.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • What does the tracker actually do per event type? Mostly it maps to a name plus params, so does it really need to know every type?
    • Is there per-type routing (some events go to vendor A only)?
    • Must events be schema-checked against a central registry for data governance?
    • Is the KMP or iOS side sharing this?
  2. Immediate mitigation: split the 2,800-line file into per-feature files within :core:analytics. Sealed allows any file in the same package and module, so merge conflicts drop immediately with zero semantic change. That buys time while we fix the fan-out.
  3. Options, ranked:
    1. Inversion: an open core contract with sealed per feature. :core:analytics defines interface AnalyticsEvent { val name: String; val params: Map<String, Any?> }. Each feature declares its own sealed interface FeedEvent : AnalyticsEvent with exhaustive mapping inside the feature. The tracker no longer switches on types. It uses the contract. Exhaustiveness lives where the types live.
    2. Keep sealed central, with a generic escape branch. Core keeps a few core events plus open class FeatureEvent(name, params) : AnalyticsEvent. Exhaustiveness in core stays (is FeatureEvent covers all features), and features extend the open branch.
    3. Codegen from a schema (YAML/JSON registry → generated event classes per module via a Gradle task or KSP). Best for governance, but the highest setup cost.
  4. How I'd verify:
    • Gradle build scans before and after: modules re-executed per event change, expected to drop from about 30 to 1–2.
    • Count merge conflicts over 4 weeks.
    • An analytics QA dashboard comparing event volumes per name before and after migration.
  5. The real tension: sealed types can't span modules by design (direct subclasses must be in the same module and package). Exhaustiveness is only valuable where code actually branches per type. The tracker doesn't need per-type logic, it needs a name and params. So the central sealed type was buying a guarantee at the wrong layer, and paying for it with a 30-module rebuild radius. "No event silently dropped" is better guaranteed by the contract: every event must provide name and params (abstract members), plus a test.
  6. Design (option 1 with a governance hook):
// :core:analytics
interface AnalyticsEvent {
    val name: String
    val params: Map<String, Any?>
}
class Tracker(private val sinks: List<AnalyticsSink>) {
    fun track(e: AnalyticsEvent) = sinks.forEach { it.send(e.name, e.params) }   // no type switch, nothing to drop
}

// :feature:feed
sealed interface FeedEvent : AnalyticsEvent {
    data class ItemViewed(val itemId: String, val position: Int) : FeedEvent {
        override val name = "feed_item_viewed"
        override val params = mapOf("item_id" to itemId, "pos" to position)
    }
    data object RefreshPulled : FeedEvent {
        override val name = "feed_refresh"
        override val params = emptyMap<String, Any?>()
    }
}

Long term: add a build-time check that every event name exists in the analytics registry. It can be a unit test per feature that reflects over FeedEvent::class.sealedSubclasses (kotlin-reflect, test-only) and asserts names against the registry file. Sealed per feature makes that enumeration possible. 7. Prevention:

  • Module-graph rule (dependency-analysis plugin or a custom Gradle check): :core:* modules must not grow per-feature types.
  • Event-name registry test in each feature.
  • Dashboards alerting on an event volume drop of more than 30% after a release.
  1. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • I lose a single place where one when lists all 310 events. Discovery moves to the registry or IDE search.
    • Per-type routing, if it exists, must become data (a destinations property) instead of a central when.
    • I would NOT keep central sealed plus else. That's the worst of both: same rebuild radius, no guarantee.
    • I would NOT use the same package across modules to "trick" sealed. It doesn't work, because the module rule is enforced.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Product wants per-vendor routing for 12 events. → Add val vendors: Set<Vendor> get() = Vendor.ALL to the contract and override it in those 12. That's data, not a central switch.
  • What if iOS shares these via KMP? → The same structure works in common code. Avoid expect sealed here, since it forces else in common code anyway.
  • Doesn't removing types from core hurt type safety at call sites? → No. Call sites still construct feature-specific sealed types. Only the tracker sees the interface.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: At a mid-size app, moving from one central sealed event file to per-feature sealed interfaces over an open contract cut the event-change rebuild from 28 modules to 2. The p50 CI time dropped by about 60% for analytics-only PRs. The registry test caught three misspelled event names in the first week.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: open interface + else, ignores the guarantee. Or doesn't know sealed can't span modules.
  • Hire: knows the module rule, proposes per-feature sealed types with a shared contract, and quantifies the build-time win.
  • Strong hire: reframes where exhaustiveness is actually useful, keeps the "never dropped" guarantee via abstract contract members plus a registry test, offers the immediate same-module file split, and lays out the trade-offs explicitly.

questions.subtopic: Evolving sealed types with external data
questions.contextHtml:
A shopping app renders its home screen from server-driven UI: a JSON list of blocks, each with a "type" discriminator. The client models it as a @Serializable sealed interface HomeBlock with 9 subtypes (banner, carousel, grid, …) decoded by kotlinx.serialization. The server team wants to launch a new "countdown" block for a sale in 10 days. Install base: 3.1M users, of which 22% are on app versions 2+ releases old, and older versions keep traffic for months. In staging, an old build fed a payload containing "countdown" shows a blank home screen, and logs:

kotlinx.serialization.json.internal.JsonDecodingException: Serializer for subclass 'countdown' is not found in the polymorphic scope of 'HomeBlock'.

The whole response fails to parse, not just one block. A PM asks, "can't we just add Countdown to the sealed interface?"
questions.promptHtml: How do you ship the new block safely to all versions, and how do you make the next one painless?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add Countdown to the sealed interface and release." New versions work, but 22%+ of users on old versions get a blank home screen on sale day. Or "the server should version the API." That's right in spirit, but it ignores the 10-day deadline and the existing install base.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Can the server filter blocks by app_version, which the client already sends in a header?
    • Is the home payload cached on device, since old cached payloads could also contain unknown types?
    • Is losing a block acceptable on old versions, or must they show a fallback?
    • Are other screens decoded the same way?
  2. Immediate mitigation (for this launch):
    • The server sends countdown only to clients whose version is at least the first version that knows it, using the version header.
    • Old clients get the same sale as a banner block, which they understand.
    • This is a server-side change with zero client risk, and it ships inside 10 days.
  3. Hypotheses / failure points ranked:
    1. Polymorphic decoding fails hard on an unknown discriminator, and one bad element fails the whole list.
    2. An exhaustive when over HomeBlock in the renderer is safe at compile time, but irrelevant to unknown runtime data.
    3. A cached payload containing an unknown type poisoning cold start offline.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Contract tests that decode fixture payloads containing unknown types for the current and previous two app versions (keep old decoder fixtures in the repo).
    • Staging: an old APK against the new payload.
    • After launch, track a metric for unknown_block_type counts by version, so the server can see who drops what.
  5. Root cause: the sealed hierarchy is closed at compile time, but the data source is open. kotlinx.serialization's sealed serializer maps a discriminator string to a known subclass serializer. With no mapping and no default registered, it throws. Because the list decoder is all-or-nothing, the entire home response fails. Exhaustive when gives no protection here: the failure happens before any when runs.
  6. Fix:
    • Short term: the server-side version gating above.
    • Long term (client): make unknown types first-class.
      • Add an Unknown subtype.
      • Register a polymorphic default deserializer so an unknown discriminator decodes to Unknown instead of throwing.
      • Make the renderer skip Unknown explicitly, and log it.
    • Verify the exact default-deserializer API against your kotlinx.serialization version. polymorphicDefaultDeserializer exists in recent versions. An alternative that doesn't depend on that is to decode each element as JsonElement and map it with a JsonContentPolymorphicSerializer, or with a per-element try/catch.
@Serializable
sealed interface HomeBlock {
    @Serializable @SerialName("banner") data class Banner(val imageUrl: String) : HomeBlock
    @Serializable @SerialName("carousel") data class Carousel(val items: List<String>) : HomeBlock
    // ... other known types
    @Serializable data class Unknown(val type: String = "") : HomeBlock   // client-only fallback, never sent by the server
}

val json = Json {
    ignoreUnknownKeys = true
    serializersModule = SerializersModule {
        polymorphicDefaultDeserializer(HomeBlock::class) { HomeBlock.Unknown.serializer() }
    }
}

@Composable
fun BlockRenderer(block: HomeBlock) = when (block) {          // still exhaustive: Unknown is a real case
    is HomeBlock.Banner -> BannerBlock(block)
    is HomeBlock.Carousel -> CarouselBlock(block)
    // ... other known types
    is HomeBlock.Unknown -> Unit                              // skip; counted via analytics elsewhere
}

With Moshi, the equivalent is PolymorphicJsonAdapterFactory.of(...).withDefaultValue(Unknown) (or withFallbackJsonAdapter). 7. Prevention:

  • A protocol rule: every server-driven sealed type must have an Unknown fallback from v1. Server-side capability or version gating stays mandatory for any new type that matters for business.
  • Contract tests with "future type" fixtures, run in CI for every release.
  • An unknown_block_type metric by version, alerting if it exceeds 1% of renders for current versions (that means we forgot to ship support).
  • The client sends a supported_blocks capability list, so the server can decide without hard-coding version numbers.
  1. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • An Unknown subtype means the renderer must handle it, which is exactly the point.
    • I would NOT model the list as List<JsonElement> everywhere and lose type safety.
    • I would NOT catch the exception at the repository level and show an empty home screen. That's the same outage with a nicer log.
    • I would NOT force-update 22% of users for a sale banner.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• An old cached payload contains a type that a newer app removed. → The same Unknown path handles it. Also version the cache key by app version or schema hash, so the cache invalidates on upgrade.
  • What about enums from the server (e.g., status)? → The same problem. Use @JsonNames/a custom serializer with an UNKNOWN constant, or decode to String and map.
  • Is adding a sealed subtype source-breaking inside the app? → Yes, intentionally. Every exhaustive when must now handle it, which is what makes the client side of the rollout safe.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A marketplace app launched a new "video" card from the server without gating. Two-release-old clients failed to parse the whole feed, and home-screen DAU on those versions dropped about 30% for 4 hours until the server rolled back. The postmortem made an Unknown fallback and capability lists mandatory for every polymorphic payload.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "add the subtype and release". Doesn't consider old versions.
  • Hire: server-side gating for the launch, plus Unknown fallback decoding, plus per-element resilience.
  • Strong hire: explains why compile-time exhaustiveness can't cover runtime data, covers cached payloads and enums, capability negotiation, contract tests with future fixtures, and metrics by version.

questions.subtopic: Value class boxing in hot paths
questions.contextHtml:
A maps/fitness app renders GPS tracks on a custom Canvas view. An engineer introduced type-safety value classes across the rendering code: @JvmInline value class Meters(val v: Double), value class Px(val v: Float), value class PointIndex(val i: Int). Within a week, the Android vitals slow-frame rate on the track screen rose from 4% to 11% on mid- and low-end devices (Snapdragon 6xx-class). p95 frame time while panning went from 14 ms to 27 ms. Track sizes are 5k–40k points. A teammate suspects the Kotlin 2.1 upgrade in the same release. That's a red herring: a build with the old compiler but the new code is equally slow. Hot code excerpt:

data class TrackPoint(val x: Px, val y: Px, val distance: Meters)

class TrackRenderer {
    var highlight: PointIndex? = null
    private val points: MutableList<TrackPoint> = mutableListOf()
    private val visible: MutableList<Px> = mutableListOf()

    fun onDraw(canvas: Canvas, project: (Meters) -> Px) {
        visible.clear()
        points.forEachIndexed { i, p ->
            val px = project(p.distance)
            if (px.v in 0f..canvas.width.toFloat()) visible += px
            if (highlight == PointIndex(i)) drawHighlight(canvas, p)
        }
        // ... draw using visible
    }
}

A Memory Profiler allocation recording during a 5-second pan shows about 2.4M allocations, with the top classes being Px, Meters, PointIndex and TrackPoint.
questions.promptHtml: Explain where the allocations come from, and how you'd keep the type safety without the cost.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Value classes are zero-cost, so it must be the compiler upgrade." Or "remove all value classes." The first is wrong. The second throws away legitimate type safety instead of fixing the few boxing sites.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Is points rebuilt per frame or only when the track changes?
    • Is project a fresh lambda per frame?
    • What's the minimum device we target for 60 fps?
    • Do we need the TrackPoint objects outside rendering (e.g., for serialization)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: none needed in production beyond the next release. This is a perf regression, not a crash. If needed, ship the old renderer behind a remote flag for low-RAM devices.
  3. Hypotheses (allocation sources), ranked:
    1. project: (Meters) -> Px is a generic Function1<Meters, Px>, so each call boxes the Meters argument and the Px return value. That's 2 boxes per point per frame.
    2. visible: MutableList<Px> boxes every visible Px.
    3. highlight: PointIndex? is a nullable primitive-backed value class, so it's boxed, and PointIndex(i) compared to it boxes per point for equals.
    4. forEachIndexed is inline, so no lambda allocation there. Not the problem.
    5. TrackPoint objects themselves: retained, not per frame, unless the track is rebuilt.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Memory Profiler allocation call stacks: box-impl frames under onDraw.
    • "Show Kotlin Bytecode" on onDraw: look for Meters.box-impl, Px.box-impl and Function1.invoke(Object).
    • A Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric scenario that pans the track for 5 s, compared before and after each change.
  5. Root cause (math): with 20k points, 60% visible, at 60 fps:
    • project boxes: 2 × 20k = 40k per frame
    • visible boxes: 12k per frame
    • PointIndex boxes: 20k per frame (the nullable highlight comparison)
    • That's about 72k per frame. A real pan renders ~30–40 fps on these devices, so about 2.5M allocations over 5 s, matching the profiler.
    • Every box is about 16–24 bytes, so roughly 1.5 MB per frame of garbage. On mid-tier ART that triggers frequent young GCs and causes main-thread allocation stalls.
  6. Fix: keep value classes at API boundaries, and use primitive storage and specialized signatures in the hot loop.
fun interface Projector { fun project(distance: Meters): Px }   // non-generic: Meters/Px stay unboxed in the signature

class TrackRenderer {
    var highlight: PointIndex = PointIndex.None                  // sentinel instead of nullable
    private var distances = DoubleArray(0)                       // structure-of-arrays storage
    private var visibleX = FloatArray(0)
    private var visibleCount = 0

    fun setTrack(points: List<TrackPoint>) {
        distances = DoubleArray(points.size) { points[it].distance.v }
        visibleX = FloatArray(points.size)
    }

    fun onDraw(canvas: Canvas, projector: Projector) {
        visibleCount = 0
        val width = canvas.width.toFloat()
        for (i in distances.indices) {
