            val px = projector.project(Meters(distances[i]))     // no box: concrete fun interface signature
            if (px.v in 0f..width) visibleX[visibleCount++] = px.v
            if (highlight.i == i) drawHighlight(canvas, i)        // primitive compare
        }
    }
}

@JvmInline value class PointIndex(val i: Int) {
    companion object { val None = PointIndex(-1) }
}

Reasoning:

  • A non-generic fun interface method has concrete parameter types, so the value classes stay unboxed in its JVM signature (the method name gets mangled, which is fine in Kotlin-only code).
  • FloatArray/DoubleArray avoid per-element boxes.
  • The sentinel removes the nullable box.
  • Expected result: allocations in onDraw near zero. I'd confirm with the same Macrobenchmark, targeting p95 back under 16 ms.
  1. Prevention:
    • A Macrobenchmark for this screen in CI, with a frame-time budget.
    • Review checklist for hot paths: no List<ValueClass>, no ValueClass? for primitive-backed classes, no generic function types taking value classes.
    • A team note: "value classes are free only when used as themselves."
    • Optionally an allocation test with Debug.startAllocCounting-style checks in a benchmark module. That API is deprecated, so a Microbenchmark's allocation count is the better choice.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • Structure-of-arrays code is less idiomatic, so I'd confine it to the renderer and keep TrackPoint for the domain layer.
    • I would NOT drop the value classes globally. Unit confusion (meters vs px) was a real bug source before.
    • I would NOT micro-optimize code outside the per-frame loop.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would Sequence help? → No. It adds iterator objects and still boxes generic elements.
  • Would making the value classes wrap Long/bit-packed values help (like Compose Offset)? → For 2D points, yes: packing x and y floats into one Long value class lets you store them in a LongArray with zero objects. That's what Compose does with Offset.
  • Is Meters(distances[i]) an allocation? → No. Constructing a value class used as itself compiles to calling constructor-impl and keeping the raw double.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A charting library adopted Dp-like value classes and Flow<Px> for gesture deltas. Gesture handling allocated about 300k boxes per second. Replacing the flow with a direct callback on a non-generic fun interface and using a NaN sentinel cut GC pauses during gestures by about 80% on low-end test devices.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: insists value classes never allocate, or removes them wholesale.
  • Hire: identifies the generic lambda, the List<Px> and nullable boxing, and fixes them with primitive arrays and sentinels.
  • Strong hire: does the allocation math to match the profiler, uses a non-generic fun interface to keep signatures unboxed, separates domain and render representations, and verifies with Macrobenchmark plus CI budgets.

questions.subtopic: Interface default methods and binary compatibility
questions.contextHtml:
Your team owns a payments SDK, published as an AAR to about 40 internal and partner apps. In SDK 4.3.0 you upgraded to Kotlin 2.2 and, "to clean up bytecode", set jvmDefault = JvmDefaultMode.NO_COMPATIBILITY. You also added fun onRetry(attempt: Int) {} with a default body to the public PaymentListener interface. Release notes said "minor, no API changes". Two days later:

  • Partner app A (Kotlin, but it bundles a prebuilt analytics plugin AAR that implements PaymentListener and was compiled against SDK 4.2 with Kotlin 1.9): java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Failed resolution of: Lcom/pay/PaymentListener$DefaultImpls; on every payment, 1.1% of sessions.
  • Partner app B (Java): no crashes. That's a red herring: it implements every method itself.
  • Your own sample app: fine, because it's rebuilt from source.

Crashlytics excerpt:

Fatal Exception: java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Failed resolution of: Lcom/pay/PaymentListener$DefaultImpls;
    at com.vendor.analytics.PayTracker.onCancelled(PayTracker.kt)
    at com.pay.internal.CheckoutController.cancel(CheckoutController.kt:88)
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review. What happened mechanically, what's the remediation, and what process changes do you make?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The partner needs to update their plugin" or "ProGuard removed the class, so add a keep rule." The first pushes the cost of our breaking change onto partners. The second is wrong: the class was never generated in 4.3.0, so there is nothing to keep.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Which SDK interfaces have default bodies? onCancelled has one, which is why the crash is there.
    • How many partner apps ship prebuilt binaries compiled against older SDK versions?
    • Did anyone run the ABI check on 4.3.0, and does it even cover DefaultImpls?
  2. Immediate mitigation:
    • Publish 4.3.1 within hours, rebuilt with jvmDefault = ENABLE (the Kotlin 2.2 default). That restores DefaultImpls and the bridges alongside the real default methods.
    • Ask partner A to bump to 4.3.1. No plugin rebuild is needed.
    • Mark 4.3.0 as "do not use" in release notes and the artifact repository.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. NO_COMPATIBILITY removed PaymentListener$DefaultImpls, which old Kotlin-compiled implementors call from their bridges. This matches the class named in the error.
    2. R8 or consumer rules stripping the class. Rejected: the class isn't in the 4.3.0 AAR at all (unzip + javap confirms).
    3. Adding onRetry broke Java implementors. Rejected for this incident: in NO_COMPATIBILITY and ENABLE modes it's a real JVM default method, so Java implementors inherit it. That's why B is fine. It would have been an AbstractMethodError risk under the old disable mode.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • javap -c on the plugin's PayTracker.onCancelled, which shows invokestatic PaymentListener$DefaultImpls.onCancelled.
    • List the 4.3.0 AAR's classes.jar contents: no $DefaultImpls. The 4.2 AAR has it.
    • Reproduce in a test app that depends on the prebuilt plugin and SDK 4.3.0, then on 4.3.1.
  5. Root cause:
    • Before 2.2 (and in disable mode), Kotlin compiled interface method bodies into PaymentListener$DefaultImpls static methods.
    • Every Kotlin class implementing the interface without overriding a method got a generated bridge, onCancelled() { PaymentListener$DefaultImpls.onCancelled(this) }.
    • The plugin was compiled against 4.2 in that mode, so its bytecode hard-references DefaultImpls.
    • In 4.3.0, NO_COMPATIBILITY emits only JVM default methods and deletes DefaultImpls. The plugin binary still calls the deleted class, so ART throws NoClassDefFoundError the first time that bridge runs, on cancel.
    • Source-level compatibility was intact. The break was purely binary, so nothing in our own CI, which rebuilds everything from source, could see it.
plugin (compiled vs 4.2, Kotlin 1.9)        SDK 4.3.0 (NO_COMPATIBILITY)
PayTracker.onCancelled()  ───invokestatic──► PaymentListener$DefaultImpls.onCancelled   ✗ (class not generated)
                                             PaymentListener.onCancelled() default ✓ (unused by old binaries)
  1. Fix:
    • Short term: 4.3.1 with ENABLE.
    • Long term:
      • Keep ENABLE for the entire 4.x line.
      • Switch to NO_COMPATIBILITY only in 5.0.0, with migration notes ("rebuild any binary implementing SDK interfaces").
      • Prefer abstract classes or fun interface callbacks for partner-implemented listeners, where we control evolution.
      • Document that new interface methods always get default bodies.
// SDK build.gradle.kts (4.x line)
kotlin {
    compilerOptions {
        jvmDefault = JvmDefaultMode.ENABLE   // default methods + DefaultImpls/bridges for old binaries
    }
}
  1. Prevention:
    • ABI validation in CI: the binary-compatibility-validator plugin, or KGP's experimental ABI validation in 2.2. I'd confirm whether it flags removed DefaultImpls. If not, add a custom check that diffs the AAR class list against the previous release.
    • A binary-compat smoke test: a test app module that depends on prebuilt implementor binaries compiled against the previous 2 SDK versions (stored as test fixtures), run against the new SDK on every release.
    • Policy: compiler-flag changes that alter emitted bytecode (jvmDefault, -Xjvm-expose-boxed, @JvmName changes, value class introduction) are API-review items and SemVer-major unless proven binary-safe.
    • Release notes template: a "binary changes" section is mandatory.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • ENABLE keeps slightly more bytecode (the bridges and DefaultImpls). For an SDK that's an acceptable cost for compatibility.
    • I would NOT ask partners to rebuild third-party plugins they don't own.
    • I would NOT hand-write a DefaultImpls class to shim it. That's fragile and invisible to the next maintainer.
    • I would NOT stay on the deprecated -Xjvm-default flag long term.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would disable have been safer? → For old binaries, yes. But in disable mode, adding onRetry breaks Java implementors (AbstractMethodError when the SDK calls it). ENABLE is the mode that's safe for both.
  • Why didn't partner A's own app code crash? → It's compiled from source against 4.3.0 with Kotlin 2.x, so its classes inherit the JVM default methods directly. Only the stale prebuilt binary had the old bridges.
  • How does D8 desugaring for older minSdk interact? → D8 desugars default methods in the app build, so it works on any API level. That's orthogonal: the missing class was never in the input.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A platform team flipped an interface-heavy library to all-default-methods in a minor version. Three client apps with vendored plugins crashed only on rarely used callbacks, so it took a week to surface. Afterwards, every release ran a "previous-binaries" compatibility app in CI, and compiler-flag diffs needed API-owner sign-off.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames ProGuard or the partner, can't explain DefaultImpls.
  • Hire: explains DefaultImpls and bridges vs JVM default methods and why NO_COMPATIBILITY broke old binaries, and ships ENABLE as the fix.
  • Strong hire: also explains why Java app B and the source-built apps were fine, why disable would have broken Java implementors when adding onRetry, why CI couldn't see it, and institutes ABI and previous-binary checks plus SemVer policy for compiler-flag changes.
